A September 1956 CIA paper reports that anti-communist demonstrations seem possible in Hungary and Poland. The heading misspells the word as Aunti-communist in the original file. Within weeks, unrest in both countries would break into the open, and Hungary's would become a full revolution.

For readers, it is the forecast before the storm, proof that the explosions of October 1956 did not catch careful watchers wholly by surprise.

Cuba was the subject of a CIA briefing prepared for the National Security Council in September 1958. Fulgencio Batista's government was weakening fast. Fidel Castro's rebels were gaining ground across the island, town by town.

The briefing gave the White House the agency's current picture of the fight for Cuba. It covered the strength of both sides and the mood of the country. Four months later Castro's forces entered Havana and Batista fled. Read today, the document shows what American leaders were told at the last stage of the old regime. It captures their view just before the revolution changed Cuba's course for good.
cia-0000132422: Growing Cuban interest in Communist China is noted in item 3 of a CIA series, dated January 3, 1960. Havana was looking for partners beyond Moscow as its revolution took shape. cia-0000132622: Support for Cuba from the whole Sino-Soviet bloc fills a CIA document dated June 5, 1960. Moscow and Beijing were rivals, yet both were backing Havana at once. Cuba played the two communist giants against each other to win aid from both. The short document surveys that support, from trade to arms, as analysts mapped it in the summer of 1960.
cia-0000135922: With a date of 6 January 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a request that a case officer give a cover briefing to undisclosed people. News and public facts shape the fight over Palestine, and Resolution A/69/22, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, deals with that field. The Assembly had read the yearly report of its Palestinian rights committee, above all the part on facts and outreach. It recalls the vote of the year before on the same work.

Wide spread of true and full facts is held to be of vital weight. Civic groups and public bodies help raise grasp of the fixed rights of the Palestinian people, above all self-rule and a state of their own. The text backs a just, lasting peace built on past deals between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.
un-ga-res-2022:
Southern Rhodesia stood on the edge of a breakaway when the General Assembly passed Resolution 2022 on 5 November 1965. The Assembly had read the reports of its decolonization team on the colony. It lists the chain of past votes. They run from the 1960 call to end colonial rule down to a text of October 1965, and a Security Council vote of May that year. None, it holds, had been put into force by Britain, the ruling power.

Fresh worry runs through the text. The chiefs of Southern Rhodesia were drawing closer to South Africa and to Portugal, in a pact to keep white minority rule in place across southern Africa. That drift, the Assembly warns, puts freedom, peace, and safety in Africa at risk. Six days later, the regime broke away.
un-ga-res-a-66-222:
Family farms feed much of the world, and Resolution 66/222 gave them a year of their own. The General Assembly had taken note of a vote by the world food body in July 2011. It recalled its own 2010 text on farm growth and food safety. Smallholder farmers, many of them women, draw a named share of praise for their needs and their work.

The vote declares an International Year of Family Farming. Such farms, it holds, are a sound base for food output that can last, and a path out of poverty for the countryside. The year would fall in 2014. A later text in this same set marks how the year was kept.

Legal shelter for the United Nations itself was set down in Resolution 22, passed by the General Assembly on 13 February 1946. Annexed to the vote stands the full text of the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations. The Assembly approves the pact and puts it to each member state for joining.

The Charter's own words frame the pact. Under Article 104, the UN holds such legal standing in each member's land as its work needs. Under Article 105, the UN, its member envoys, and its staff hold such shelter from local law as their tasks demand. The pact spells out what that means in courts, taxes, and bags of mail. It is still in force today.

The catalog names no subject for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room. The record is one of the February documents of a force that had weeks of preparation left. The force had no way to know how the operation would end.
cia-0000136722: Spanish records of Brigade 2506 hold this document under an estimated date of 1 January 1961. An earlier summary described a European war agenda and invasion planning for this item; that material belongs to another era and another war, and it is removed. plos-pone-0000022:
Janine Stubbe, Dorret Boomsma, Jacqueline Vink, and co-authors asked in 2006 how much of our exercise habit is written in our genes. They used twins, the classic tool for splitting nature from nurture: identical twins share all their genes, fraternal twins only half. Their sample was huge, 37,051 twin pairs drawn from seven countries.

Comparing exercise participation across those pairs let the team estimate the genetic pull on whether a person stays active. Habits like exercise are usually blamed on willpower and surroundings; a strong genetic signal reframes the advice doctors give. The cross-country design also shows whether the genetic effect holds across cultures, not just in one population.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d22: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on August 11, 1943, as the two men prepared to meet at Quebec within days. His message is Document 22 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Quebec Conference, where the allies would argue out the next year's strategy, opened on August 14. The record for this note names no subject. It stands in the Foreign Relations series among the papers that framed the autumn's larger meetings at Cairo and Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d122: On November 12, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek, from the start of his voyage east. The letter is Document 122 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang would reach Cairo by air from China, and the meeting of the three leaders there opened on November 22. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d222:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt sent a short most-secret telegram from Ankara on 16 November 1943, number 1880. It reports a small press item with a pointed meaning. Turkish censors had told foreign reporters that morning that no more dispatches about the battle for the island of Leros would be passed.

Steinhardt reads the ban as a wish to hide the growing help Turkey was quietly giving the British on the Aegean islands, where German reinforcements had landed and the defenders were outnumbered. As support, he notes that lighthouses on the Turkish coast near Leros had been put out the night before, so British boats could land Greek guerrillas on the island in darkness.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d322:
The secretaries of the Combined Chiefs of Staff issued a note, paper C.C.S. 407/1, at Cairo on 26 November 1943. It lists the subjects, left over from the Moscow Conference, that the American and British military missions in Moscow should now take up with the Soviet authorities.

Three heads are set out in detail. On shuttle bomber bases, the missions are to ask when the Soviets will name some ten bases for bombing runs from Britain and Italy, and when service crews may be sent in. On air transport, a weekly service is sought on three routes, by Alaska, by Britain, and by Tehran. On weather, the West asks for Soviet weather ciphers, offering its own in exchange, with named regions if the full swap is refused. The missions must report progress to the chiefs from time to time.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d422:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Tehran on 5 December 1943, number 1090, with news of another broken release date. The tightly held Declaration on Iran had appeared in print a day early.

The Persian-language newspaper Friend of Iran, published by the Soviet Embassy's press section, carried the full text of the declaration that morning. So far as Dreyfus knows, no other Tehran morning paper printed it in any form. On learning of the Soviet paper's publication, Prime Minister Soheily released the text to the Tehran press himself, and it will appear in all the afternoon papers. Hurley and Dreyfus had understood definitely that nothing was to be released by anyone until eight the next night, Moscow time, and the British and Americans will still hold to that hour.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d522:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 20, 1943, back in Washington after the Tehran and Cairo journey. Hopkins, the President's special assistant, worked from the White House rather than from the State Department. The Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Hopkins and Hull represented two different styles of Roosevelt's government: the personal envoy and the cabinet secretary. Business between them had to be joined up after a trip on which Hopkins had seen everything and Hull had seen the cables. A message in this channel shows that joining-up in progress. It also marks the summit season closing into ordinary, if urgent, administration.
frus-1944-quebec-d22:
A further Churchill message to President Roosevelt is dated August 8, 1944, making a dense packet for a single day. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume alongside its companion.

Same-day companions in this file usually divide a military question from a political one, letting each be argued cleanly. August 1944 supplied plenty of both, from the race for Paris to the first arguments over Germany's future. For readers, this message rewards being read with its pair, as the two men themselves would have done, across one crowded day of a collapsing front.
frus-1944-quebec-d122:
State Department planners prepared this top-secret briefing paper, titled "Anglo-American-Russian Relations," for the Quebec Conference in September 1944. It was annexed to a memorandum Secretary Hull sent Roosevelt. The paper asks how the three great powers will relate once the war ends, and what role Britain will try to play between Washington and Moscow.

Its core is a long quotation from Admiral Leahy's letter of May 16, 1944. Leahy argued that keeping the three powers united was the cardinal aim of policy. Russia's strength was rising fast; America could defend Britain but could not defeat Russia in Europe. The paper urges blocking rival spheres of influence and drawing the Soviet Union into the planned world organization.
frus-1944-quebec-d222:
Hull returned to the meat contract the next day, September 13, 1944, with additional observations of mounting anger. The embassy in Buenos Aires reported that Britain's Ministry of Food had told the Argentines it would sign a two-year contract at current prices. Britain would buy the entire exportable surplus for four years, prices re-examined at two. The word from London, Hull noted, came as a great relief to the Colonels.

To Hull, Britain treated the Argentine Fascist threat as minor policy; to America it was major. Failure, he warned, would give the Nazis a powerful center to renew their fight in this hemisphere. Given America's enormous aid, asking Britain to forego petty commercial advantages from a Fascist government was not asking too much.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d22: The same day he wrote Stalin, 18 November 1944, Roosevelt also sent Churchill a message, filed as document 22. It appears in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Handling both allies on one day was the president's routine that fall, and the paired letters let readers compare what each partner was told.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d122:
Slow down, the President told his Secretary of State on 20 October 1944. Roosevelt's top secret memorandum answers Hull's paper of 29 September on planning Germany's treatment. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Preparations are all very well, Roosevelt writes, but speed is not essential now. He dislikes detailed plans for a country the allies do not yet occupy; a week, a month, or several months may pass first. One warning stands out. The European Advisory Commission is advisory, and he and the Secretary are not bound by its advice. Some points are clear already, demilitarization among them, and those can be approved at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d222:
Will Clayton warned against sweetening the lend-lease terms for Moscow in this 20 January 1945 paper. The assistant secretary's comments, addressed to Stettinius, are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. They answer proposals lately made by Secretary Morgenthau on postwar trade with the Soviet Union.

The Treasury would now offer the 3(c) supplementary agreement without interest charges. Clayton objects that Washington told the Soviet negotiators, in full good faith and with Treasury agreement, that its last 3(c) offer was final. Better terms were said to be barred on legal and other grounds. To come back now with the same offer minus interest would tell Moscow that last summer's word was not true. It might kindle afresh the old Soviet suspicion of American good faith.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d322:
President Roosevelt's party reached the Crimea on February 3, 1945, and the official log of the trip tells the day hour by hour. His plane, guarded by five fighters, landed at Saki airfield after a 1,375-mile flight from Malta. Foreign Commissar Molotov, Secretary Stettinius, and Ambassador Harriman waited on the ground. Stalin had not yet arrived in the Crimea.

Roosevelt stayed aboard until Churchill's plane came in some twenty minutes later. The log names the Secret Service agents of the advance party and notes one escort fighter that turned back to Athens with engine trouble. Such logs anchor the conference story in times, miles, and weather.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d422:
Eleven American questions, eleven Soviet answers: this memorandum of February 9, 1945, sums up Antonov's replies for the United States Chiefs of Staff. On operations, there was no change but delay. Troops meant to move east at the New Year were engaged in the central sector of the Eastern Front.

On supply, Stalin said the Pacific sea route would be required. Foodstuffs and petroleum products topped the need. Some air transport would probably be wanted, though its capacity was small. The memo, written the same afternoon, turns a secret oral briefing into a planning document. Each short answer fed American timetables for the Pacific war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d22:
Keep the trip quiet: Grew's memorandum of May 21, 1945, records a telephone call with Stettinius about the Hopkins mission. Grew told the Secretary that Hopkins was going to Moscow with Harriman, and that the fact should stay quiet until Hopkins arrived. The Secretary asked whether they were leaving together. Harriman was leaving that day; Hopkins would follow in a couple of days, with Bohlen.

Harriman had wanted to clear the trip with the Secretary, Grew added, but it had come to a head very quickly. Such a visit would be very helpful, he thought, since Hopkins seemed to have Stalin's confidence. The President had approved it. The memo shows the mission arranged in hours, by telephone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d122:
President Truman told Stalin on July 5, 1945, that the press ban at Terminal would be announced that day. His secret message, number 309, is document 122 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had proposed the advance announcement so that newspapers would not send top reporters to Berlin for nothing.

Truman writes that, in line with their understanding, he is announcing that the press will not be allowed at Terminal. All that will be issued, he says, will be such official communiqués as the three governments decide on from time to time. He adds that a similar message has gone to Churchill. The three-power agreement kept the conference sealed, with news released only in joint statements.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d222:
A State Department briefing paper made the case for restoring France to great-power rank. Its extracts are printed as document 222 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper, from Truman's briefing book, surveys France's return to world councils since her liberation in 1944.

So will her contribution to a peaceful world. This will happen if her wish for full partnership is met by anticipation rather than by tardy or grudging compliance. The extracts trace the steps so far. They include recognition of her government and a promised permanent Security Council seat. They also include a full share in the control machinery for Germany, including her own occupation zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d322:
Prepared for the President's briefing book, an undated paper sets out how the United States should handle Soviet economic moves in Eastern Europe. Its recommendations ask Truman to seek a Soviet pledge on several points. The first concerns property owned by Americans in the countries Moscow's armies occupied.

The paper asks that removals of such capital equipment stop, that gear already taken be returned, and that owners who cannot get it back be paid promptly and in full. It also asks free entry and travel for Americans, and no deals giving the Soviet Union a sole grip on trade or raw materials in those countries.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d422:
Ruhr coal figures fill Murphy's cable to Clayton of June 29, 1945, an informal summary of the situation. Stocks on hand, he reports, total between six and seven million tons on the surface. Production has jumped to 60,000 tons of marketable coal daily, beyond what the mines themselves burn.

That rate equals about a million and a half marketable tons a month. Murphy's sources estimate it will rise to four million tons monthly within two months. He also passes on a complaint: early delay owed much to a poor choice of British military personnel, when the 21st Army Group assigned some 4,000 officers and men to the task.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d522:
Polish economic hopes are reported in Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 26, 1945. At lunch on June 23 with Bierut, Osóbka-Morawski, and Mikołajczyk, he had recalled their earlier talk, in which the Poles emphasized their hope for economic assistance from the United States. He suggested an informal discussion of what they visualized, which he could report to his government.

Relief and rehabilitation, Harriman explained, would be dealt with by UNRRA, and in the medical field to some extent by the American Red Cross. Reconstruction, he said, must be dealt with on a business basis. Bierut readily recognized this principle, and said the new Polish government would wish to make a commercial treaty with the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d622:
Edward Wolf, liaison man in Washington for the U.S. reparations team, wired Edwin Pauley in Moscow on June 30, 1945. The secret message is document 622 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It passes on oil figures from Ralph Davies of the Petroleum Administration for War.

Davies put the 1946 surplus oil of Russian-held Eastern Europe at some 60,000 barrels a day above local needs. Rumania alone accounts for 47,000 of that figure. Against it, Western and Mediterranean Europe would draw some 292,000 barrels a day from Anglo-U.S. sources in late 1945. Use of the eastern surplus, Davies argued, would ease a tight world supply. It would also save much tanker space if the oil moved west by land or from Constanta by ship.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-22:
A United States delegation memorandum sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 19, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its purpose was to fix the agenda for the heads of government that afternoon.

Five subjects were recommended in order. First came the Control Council's authority in German political questions, on an approved redraft. Poland came second, with a British paper sent to a subcommittee for drafting changes. If that group reported by four o'clock, Poland would be ready that day. Third came the disposition of the German fleet and merchant ships, on a Russian paper. Spain came fourth, again on a Russian paper proposing a joint policy toward Franco. Fifth came the carrying out of the Yalta declaration on liberated Europe and the satellite states.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-122:

In Cohen's pages the reader follows remarks almost as spoken. He noted not just conclusions but the path to them. That path matters, since Potsdam's phrases were argued over for years. The notes show a careful lawyer guarding each commitment as it was made.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d722:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d822:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d922: Drafters prepared this short report for the Economic Sub-Committee at Potsdam, left undated in the files. It admits failure in plain terms. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1022:

He asks for a study of international ownership of the Ruhr and Saar resources. He also attacks a plan to sever the Ruhr and Rhineland as a protectorate. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1122:

cherry-garrard-worst-journey-1922:

eratosthenes-fragments-bernhardy-1822:
Eratosthenes ran the great library at Alexandria and measured the girth of the Earth with shadows and sums. His own books are lost, and only pieces quoted by later writers survive. Eratosthenica, in Gottlieb Bernhardy's 1822 collection, gathers those scattered fragments in one place.

His lost Geography founded the craft of mapping the world on a grid of lines. The fragments show his work on place, measure, myth, and the size of the inhabited earth. Scholars rebuild his thought piece by piece from these scraps. Bernhardy's file has been the base for that hard work since 1822.
crowley-diary-of-a-drug-fiend-1922:
Two young lovers slide into cocaine and heroin in Crowley's novel of 1922. The Diary of a Drug Fiend follows their fall, their craving, and their hard road back. The book's frank drug scenes made Crowley infamous in the British press of the day.

achad-qbl-brides-reception-1922:
Charles Stansfeld Jones, who wrote as Frater Achad, was Crowley's prized student until he redrew the Tree of Life. Q B L, or The Bride's Reception, printed in 1922, is his first major work of Kabbalah. In it he shifts the letters and paths of the Tree to new places.

ouspensky-tertium-organum-1922:
Peter Ouspensky argued that the mind needs a new organ of thought to grasp the world whole. Tertium Organum, in its English form of 1922, makes that case at full length. Its title claims a third canon of thought, past the logic of Aristotle and Bacon.

The fourth dimension is his key: time and space as we feel them are slices of a fuller world. Dreams, art, and mystic sight become clues to that wider realm, not mere fog. bradley-on-the-gorilla-trail-1922:
Mary Hastings Bradley went up into the Virunga volcanoes in 1922 and wrote one of the first gorilla books. On the Gorilla Trail tells her search for the mountain gorilla in its cloud forests. She was among the first women to make that hard trek.

With her husband Herbert, she camps, tracks, and at last stands close to the great apes. Her eye is sharp for camp life, porters, and the green world of the hills. The book opened the gorilla's country to a wide body of readers. It stands as a pioneer woman's tale of exploration.
barns-wonderland-of-the-eastern-congo-19:
Thomas Alexander Barns wandered the snow-crowned volcano country of the eastern Congo in 1922. The Wonderland of the Eastern Congo is his tale of that rich, wild borderland. Barns was a hunter and collector who knew the lakes and hills at first hand.

Gorillas, elephants, and the peoples of the hills fill his bright pages. The land he crossed was then at the dawn of gorilla science, still half tale to the West. His book catches the last romantic years of African exploration. It is a hunter's hymn to a country of fire mountains and great apes.
machen-secret-glory-1922:
A schoolboy touches a higher world in Machen's novel of 1922, The Secret Glory. Ambrose Meyrick endures a dull, harsh school while his soul feeds on Grail lore and the tales of saints. The holy hides in the schoolroom in Machen's telling.

Meyrick's secret life of vision sets him apart from masters and boys alike, and draws scorn he barely feels. Machen pours his own school years and his Grail faith into the tale. The book is the full flower of the Rosicrucian thread in his work. It finds glory where the world sees only a drab boy.
jersey-devil-evening-world-wombat-1909-0:

Its wags sort the beast with mock care and place it, at last, as a wombat: a stout beast of the far south that no more flies than a pig.

The joke needs the panic to land, and that panic was real. The piece is a prime scrap of how press both fed and mocked the wave. It shows the craze at its peak.
boy-of-bilson-1622:
Richard Baddeley busts a false seer in The Boy of Bilson, his tract of 1622. William Perry, a boy of Bilson, had seemed to be held by a foul soul: fits, strange words, and awe struck priests who sought to cast the soul out. Crowds came to watch the rite. Then the boy, in 1620, owned the whole thing was a sham taught to him by the priests for their church's fame.

Baddeley prints the tale and the boy's own words in full. The case cut both ways in the faith rows of the age. The tract is a prime bust text.
luschan-volker-rassen-sprachen-1922:
Felix von Luschan, a German sage of the study of man, struck at the race scheme of his day in this book of 1922. Its title means peoples, races, and tongues, in German. Luschan had spent years in the field and in charge of a great store of skulls.

He holds that races are not fixed types set for all time by blood. Groups mix, shift, and blur, he says, and the neat boxes of the schools leak at each seam. His book is a bold charge on the race frame from a man at the heart of the field.
osborn-hesperopithecus-1922:

Osborn hails the tooth as the first ape like primate found in America. He knows the proof is thin, yet he puts the claim in print with his great name on it. The paper is the start of the most famed false claim in the study of man's rise.

watkins-early-british-trackways-1922:
Alfred Watkins put out Early British Trackways in 1922. He was a trader and a keen walker of the Hereford hills. On one June day in 1921 he thought he saw straight lines link old sites. Mounds, moats, camps, and mark stones seemed to fall on one line.

Watkins calls such a line a ley and says old tracks ran along them. He gives maps and tales of sight lines across the land. Most experts in the field doubt the claim, but the idea took hold. The book is the start point of the whole ley line debate.
burckhardt-travels-syria-1822:
John Lewis Burckhardt roamed Syria and the Holy Land in the years before 1822. His Travels came out that year, after his early death. He rode in Arab dress and wrote with a sharp eye. The book holds two finds that made his name last.

Burckhardt gives the first full tale in Europe of Baalbek and its huge cut stones. Three stones in one wall, the trilithon, weigh close to a thousand tons each in bulk. He also tells of his ride to Petra, the lost rock city of the Nabataeans. The book opened the Levant to new study.
heindel-rosicrucian-philosophy-qa-1922:
Max Heindel set his Rosicrucian Philosophy in Questions and Answers in 1922. The form is plain: a short ask, then a full reply. The book serves as a mate to his Cosmo-Conception. It deals with the points new hands ask most.

Karma, birth anew, and the life past death fill much of the text. Heindel tells what the dead see, how the soul grows, and how to live well. Health, food, and prayer get plain, firm words too. The book shows the school at work on real doubts of real folk.
boehme-way-to-christ-1622:
Jakob Boehme was a German shoe maker who saw great light in prayer. The Way to Christ, from 1622, holds his short works for the plain soul. True change of heart comes first in his plan. The book is the best first step into his hard, bright thought.

Short tracts deal with true grief for sin, new birth, and yield to God. One more tells of the life past sense, where the soul rests in Christ. Boehme writes as a guide, not a sage on a throne. The book's warm tone won him fans all over the North.
boehme-signature-of-all-things-1622:

doyle-coming-of-the-fairies-1922:

frazer-golden-bough-abridged-1922:

shakespeare-othello-1622:

tolstoy-war-and-peace-maude-1922:

Pierre, Andrei, and Natasha live through Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 and its wars. Balls, hunts, and drawing rooms alternate with Borodino and the burning of Moscow in 1812. Tolstoy asks how great events truly happen, and scorns the great-man view of past times. Essays on history interrupt the tale and dare readers to rethink war and power itself. defoe-moll-flanders-1722:
Daniel Defoe published Moll Flanders in 1722, the great criminal autobiography of English fiction in prose. The book is a founding picaresque of the modern novel, told in Moll's own voice. Defoe knew Newgate and the London underworld, and his detail smells of both worlds in truth.

Moll, born in Newgate prison, is raised by a mayor's family and seduced young in Colchester. Five husbands, bigamy, incest by chance, and a career of theft fill her long, busy life. She grows rich as a thief, is caught, and is transported to Virginia with her Lancashire husband. There she prospers honestly at last and repents in comfort, if not quite in sorrow. The tale's energy and moral blur still spark argument three centuries on.
defoe-journal-of-the-plague-year-1722:
Daniel Defoe published A Journal of the Plague Year in 1722, a pseudo-documentary of 1665 London. The book invented the documentary novel and disaster reportage in English prose for later writers everywhere. Defoe was five in the plague year and rebuilt it from bills, tales, and records.

A saddler, H. F., stays in London as plague kills tens of thousands around his parish. He records bills of mortality, shut houses with red crosses, pits, and fleeing crowds in Aldgate. Tales of nurses, quacks, and piper anecdotes break the grim tally of the dead each week. Fear of policy, such as shutting houses, runs beside fear of the disease itself in London. The calm, factual voice makes the horror feel close, modern, and hard to shake.
defoe-colonel-jack-1722:

Back in Europe he fights in wars, weds four wives, and kills a man in a duel. Ever seeking to be a gentleman, he is haunted by the thefts of his boyhood in London.
