Heidi Noels and colleagues showed that auto ubiquitination induced degradation of MALT1-API2 prevents BCL10 destabilization in MALT lymphoma, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The translocation t(11;18) is the most frequent chromosomal aberration in MALT lymphoma and results in constitutive NF-kB activity via an API2-MALT1 fusion protein. Properties of the reciprocal MALT1-API2 product were never investigated, as it was assumed absent or rapidly lost in tumor cells.

The reciprocal product degrades itself, protecting BCL10. That balance shapes signaling strength in lymphoma. Fusion biology is more two sided than thought. Details may suggest therapeutic leverage. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0005422:
Paul Vigne, Michel Tauc, and Christian Frelin studied fruit flies and low oxygen in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When blood flow returns to tissue that has lacked oxygen, the fresh oxygen can itself cause harm. That problem shapes how bad heart and blood vessel disease becomes.

The team used newly hatched adult male fruit flies, which cope well without oxygen. Flies kept on a very strict diet were better protected from harm when oxygen returned. The result points to diet and body chemistry as factors that can change how tissue survives a lack of oxygen.
plos-pone-0005522:
Evelyn Teran, Aron Branscomb, and Joni Seeling studied a protein that can both block and boost a growth pathway, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The Wnt pathway guides development and can drive tumours when it runs unchecked. A protein called Dpr helps set its strength.

The team showed that Dpr works as a switch with two states. In one state it holds Wnt signals back; after a chemical tag is added by another enzyme, it pushes the signals forward. A two-way switch like this lets cells fine-tune a powerful pathway.
plos-pone-0005622:
Hanane Agherbi and co-authors studied a tumour suppressor region in aging cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. One DNA region, INK4a/ARF, holds three genes that block tumours. It is shut down in many human cancers, and the ways it is controlled were not fully known.

The team showed that a protein complex called Polycomb silences the region as cells age into senescence. They also linked that silencing to when the region's DNA is copied. The timing detail may explain why the region's loss is so common in cancer. Senescence is a guard against cancer, so the silencing that comes with it has a double edge worth study.
plos-pone-0005722:
Roy Blum and co-authors compared gene activity in young and adult prostate stem cells in 2009. Stem cells from the prostate may hold clues to how prostate cancer starts. The team read the full set of active genes in both fetal and adult stem cells.

They found a shared core set of control genes in both stages. Some of those same controls go wrong in cancer. That overlap makes the stem cell program a map for spotting cancer's first steps. The study also names new signal paths tied to these cells, giving labs fresh targets to test in prostate disease.
plos-pone-0005822:
Ethan Mann and co-authors showed in 2009 how the release and breakdown of DNA shapes the films Staphylococcus aureus builds. These biofilms coat surfaces and implants, shielding bacteria from drugs and immunity. DNA spilled from dead cells acts as a glue in the film.

Genes that control cell lysis, including cidA, govern how much DNA is freed. Other factors chew that DNA up, loosening the film as it matures. Tuning either side changes how the film holds together. That suggests anti-biofilm strategies aimed at the DNA glue, a growing idea in implant infection care.
plos-pone-0006422:
Maria Garcia and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Rb, a protein best known for holding back tumors. Rb helps control the cell cycle, cell growth into mature forms, and the start of cancer. The team asked whether Rb also plays a part when a virus infects a cell and the NF-kB pathway switches on.

Their title states the finding plainly: turning on that pathway after virus infection requires Rb to be present. A tumor guard thus doubles as part of the immune alarm. The work widens what Rb is thought to do inside cells. It also links cancer biology with the study of virus defense.
plos-pone-0006522:
Jason Locasale and Alejandro Wolf-Yadlin rebuilt cell signal networks from protein data in PLOS ONE in 2009. New tools can now weigh many proteins at once with care. They can track tags added to proteins as signals move through a cell. The authors used a method called maximum entropy to infer the network from such data, adding as few guesses as they could.

Their method rebuilds live signal networks from large sets of protein measures. A clear map shows where signals branch and where a drug might act. The approach suits the big, noisy data sets that new tools produce. It is a tool for systems biology, the study of the cell as a whole.
plos-pone-0006622:
Adam Pluskota and co-authors used see-through worms to watch tiny particles at work in PLOS ONE in 2009. Uses of nanotechnology are growing fast. Yet little is known about how built nanoparticles act inside animals with many cells. The team used the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, a tiny worm whose body is clear. That clarity lets one watch where particles go in a living animal.

Their title says these particle-body interactions become clear to see, and that silica nanoparticles harm the worms' reproduction. Early proof of harm in a model worm guides safer design of nanomaterials. The study helps build the safety science that the nano age needs.
plos-pone-0009422:
Jung Nyeo Chun and co-authors published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hsp60 is a helper protein usually found inside mitochondria. Some of it, though, sits free in the cell's main body, the cytosol. There it seems to help cancer cells survive.

The team traced how cytosolic Hsp60 keeps cancer cells alive. It works by regulating IKK, a controller of the survival pathway NF-kappaB. With that pathway on, cancer cells resist signals telling them to die. A helper protein moonlighting outside its usual home thus becomes a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0009522:
Zhike Zi, Wolfram Liebermeister, and Edda Klipp measured a yeast stress pathway with care in PLOS ONE in 2010. Yeast cells face fast swings in the saltiness of their surroundings. A pathway led by the protein Hog1 helps them adapt. The team changed osmotic stress up and down over time. They tracked how the pathway answered each swing.

Quantitative measures like these let modelers test their math against real cell behavior. The pathway did not just switch on and off. It graded its response to the pattern of stress. The study shows how a single cell computes a fitting reply to a shifting world.
plos-pone-0009622:
Robert Thacker and co-authors surveyed sponges on a giant Caribbean atoll in PLOS ONE in 2010. Saba Bank, in the Netherlands Antilles, is one of the largest atolls on Earth. Its reefs were little studied despite their size. A multi disciplinary team sampled the bank for its living diversity. Sponges were a focus, since they are diverse and ecologically key on reefs.

The survey gave a first full account of the bank's sponge fauna. Many species were recorded there for the first time. Such an inventory is the base for any plan to protect the area. It also shows how much life a single remote reef system can hold.
plos-pone-0010422:
Philippa Mitchell and colleagues used a tiny worm to separate fresh from lasting responses to alcohol in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long drinking followed by stopping brings withdrawal: anxiety, agitation, sometimes seizures. A small drink relieves it, which traps people in dependence. The worm C. elegans shows its own versions of these responses. The team applied behavior tests and genetics to tell acute reactions from chronic adaptation.

Small signaling molecules called neuropeptides played different roles in the two phases. That split matters because treatments for binge effects may not touch dependence. A worm that separates the phases gives drug research a sorting tool. Its simple genetics let single molecules be blamed or cleared fast. Alcohol's grip, the study suggests, is at least two grips.
plos-pone-0010522:
Jessica Lou and co-workers found that DNA-damaging agents can block production of a low-oxygen response protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells sense low oxygen through a factor called HIF. It pairs an oxygen-sensitive part, HIF-1alpha, with a steady partner. HIF lets cells and tissues adapt when oxygen runs low. Tumors exploit it to grow blood vessels. The team asked how DNA-damaging treatments, common in cancer care, affect it.

Those agents cut the making of new HIF-1alpha protein. That side effect could help explain why some treatments starve tumors. It might also harm normal tissue healing after therapy. Either way, a hidden link between DNA damage and oxygen sensing is exposed. The study connects two major fields of cancer biology.
plos-pone-0010622:
Kai Wang and colleagues studied the first cell split in mouse embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A fertilized egg cluster soon divides into inner cells, which form the baby, and outer cells, which form the placenta. Two gene switches, Oct4 and Cdx2, push cells toward opposite fates.

Cdx2 must silence Oct4 in the outer cells. The team found that a helper protein, Brg1, is required for that silencing to work. Without Brg1, Oct4 stayed on in cells meant to become placenta. The result shows how early embryos lock in their first major decision.
plos-pone-0010722:
Matthew Johns and colleagues studied flu shots in US military personnel during the 2009 pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A new H1N1 virus spread worldwide that year. The vaccine against it arrived late, so many people relied on whatever protection the earlier seasonal shot might give.

The team tracked illness among service members with known shot records. Earlier seasonal vaccination gave, at best, limited protection against the pandemic strain. Some groups showed a small benefit; others showed none. Honest numbers like these help planners avoid false comfort and push for faster pandemic vaccine production.
plos-pone-0010822:
Zhichao Jin and colleagues audited research methods in Chinese medical journals across a decade, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clinical research output from China grew enormously between 1998 and 2008. Growth in count says nothing about quality. Sound design and correct statistics are what make a study's answer believable.

The audit sampled journals from both years and graded design and analysis. Standards had improved, yet common flaws persisted in both rounds. Misused tests and unclear designs still weakened many papers. An honest baseline tells editors and trainers exactly which skills to teach next, instead of assuming progress.
plos-pone-0010922:
Harish Nagarajan, Jessica Butler, Anna Klimes and co-authors published this genome sequencing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. New sequencing machines read DNA fast but only in short scraps, and no one had yet assembled a complete genome from those scraps alone, without help from older methods. The team aimed to prove it could be done.

Their four-phase strategy combined two short-read technologies to build the full genome of a Geobacter variant prized for producing unusually strong electric current at electrodes. The finished assembly covered the bacterium's whole chromosome, about three point seven million letters. Nagarajan and colleagues deliver a proof of principle that complete genomes can come from short reads only. That lowers the cost of sequencing microbes that turn waste or fuel into electricity.
plos-pone-0011022:
Yun Lu, Christopher Futtner, Jason Rock and co-authors published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. SOX2 is a stem cell factor found at high levels in some lung tumors. The authors asked whether too much SOX2 is merely a passenger in those tumors or a driver capable of causing them.

They confirmed SOX2 overexpression in human squamous lung tumors and some adenocarcinomas, then built mice that switch on extra Sox2 in lung lining cells during development or in adulthood. Both settings produced extensive overgrowth, and the smallest airways remodeled into a trachea-like layered lining. Over the following months about half the highest-expressing mice developed carcinoma. Lu and colleagues prove SOX2 overexpression is oncogenic in lung, a stem cell program turned cancer driver.
plos-pone-0011122:
Chatterjee, Adak, Singh and colleagues sampled high mountain air in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their station sat in the northeast Himalayas in India, far above most towns. They analyzed the fine particles floating there, called aerosols, and what those particles are made of.

The chemistry tells which particles arise locally and which drift in from far away. Even remote peaks receive pollution carried on winds from lower land. That reach matters for climate, since particles affect clouds and sunlight. The data give a rare baseline for a region where long term air records are scarce.
plos-pone-0011222:
Vala, Martins, Imaizumi and colleagues gave low radiation doses in cancer tests for PLOS ONE in 2010. Radiation usually aims to kill tumors, but the team tested whether small doses could have the opposite effect. In their experiments, low doses were checked for effects on tumor growth, spread and blood vessel formation.

Low doses promoted tumor growth and spread by boosting new vessel formation. That paradox urges caution when planning radiotherapy near tumors. Scatter doses to nearby tissue might aid vessels that feed remaining cancer. The finding could reshape how treatment doses and fields are planned to avoid that risk.
plos-pone-0011322:
Cohen, Lawrence and Margulies modeled septic lungs in dishes for PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung air sac cells taken from septic rats were grown in culture. In sepsis, these cells' tight seals loosen and the lung barrier leaks. The team asked whether cultured cells keep that septic behavior outside the body.

The cultured cells did mimic the living septic lung, with altered junctions and barrier function. A faithful dish model lets researchers test sepsis treatments without whole animal experiments at every step. It speeds the search for drugs that restore the lung barrier. The model also confirms that sepsis leaves a lasting mark on the cells themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1222:
Harriman wrote to the Secretary of State on 31 July 1945, from his post as ambassador to the Soviet Union. The cable went out two days before Potsdam closed. The Moscow embassy's word still mattered as the final terms were fixed.

Harriman had dealt with Stalin's government for two years. His judgments on Soviet aims carried a tested weight in Washington. A late dispatch from his hand belongs to the summit's endgame picture. It shows the Moscow post at work to the last, feeding the secretary the capital's mood while the deal was sealed in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1322:
The Economic Subcommittee reported again on 24 July 1945. Its reports carried the staff-level work on Germany's economy up to the foreign ministers. This second report in the volume came a week into the summit, as the money terms hardened.

The group's charge covered the state of German industry, food, and trade, and the rules the peace would set for each. Its findings fed the protocol's money clauses. This report is the expert layer speaking a second time. Read with the first report, it shows the economic brief growing as the bargaining narrowed toward terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1422:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam submitted a text on 14 July 1945, in the volume's closing run of conference papers. Three Soviet texts in the volume bear that date, the eve of the leaders' arrival at Potsdam.

Tabling several texts at once is a way of setting the agenda before others can. The Soviet side came to Germany with its program written out, and these papers are that program in pieces. For readers, the worth lies in sequence: Soviet asks first, then the talks, then the signed results. This text is one piece of the opening hand Moscow played at the last wartime summit.
frus-1945-50-intel-d22:
Morton Chiles of the FBI sent a memorandum to Director Hoover on 2 October 1945. It is one of the bureau's inside papers printed in the volume's opening run. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Field and headquarters men fed Hoover a stream of reports on the shifting intelligence scene. Chiles's memorandum adds a staff voice to the director's own letters, widening the picture of how the bureau watched its rivals. Readers building the FBI side of the story should gather these inside papers together. They show an agency that treated the bureaucratic fight of 1945 as seriously as any case, and staffed it accordingly.
frus-1945-50-intel-d122: A memorandum for the record, dated 8 August 1946, was written on the dispute's busiest day. That day, the National Intelligence Authority and Director Hoover both sent letters to the attorney general. Memoranda for the record fix a talk or an act in writing while it is fresh. The bare title names no author. So the paper's weight comes from its date, and from its place in the run of August papers that settled the hemisphere question.
frus-1945-50-intel-d222:
Dated 19 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) to the National Security Council. Readers meet it as document 222 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. That season, the talk in Washington was of one big law to join up defense, foreign policy, and intelligence.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d322:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 10" heads a text dated 30 July 1947. It survives in print as document 322 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act was moving through Congress that year, and it would soon replace the wartime setup with the CIA.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Later directives amend or kill earlier ones, so the number and date fix this one's place in the chain. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d422:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 4 was issued on 12 December 1947. It is document 422 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

These directives, called NSCIDs, were the standing rules of the new intelligence system. The Council used them to divide duties among the CIA and the older department and service shops. A directive from the first months of the CIA shows the rules being written while the work was already under way. The first directives leaned on the wartime OSS as a model, even as they broke new ground.
frus-1861-d22:
Henry Sanford reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 May 1861. The dispatch is document 22 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

May 1861 was the month Britain set its neutral stance toward the American war. Small posts like Brussels felt the shift at once in trade and talk. Sanford's late May letter shows a minor capital reacting to choices made in the great ones. Small courts felt each shift of the great powers at once, and Sanford read those shifts well. He read the small signs of a small court with a big court's worth of care.
frus-1861-d122:
Writing to Paris on 4 May 1861, William H. Seward framed orders for William Dayton. The letter is document 122 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By May, Dayton was settling into the Paris legation. Seward's orders framed his talks with the French foreign office. France would move only with Britain, but its emperor's lean toward the South made Paris a post of constant watch. France and Britain acted in step that spring, which doubled the weight of Paris news. Step in step action by the two great powers shaped every smaller court's choice.
frus-1861-d222:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 15 May 1861, addressed to Mr. Fogg. It was printed as Document 222 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d22:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 11 February 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 22 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d122:
In a report dated 7 August 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 122 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d222:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, addressed William Stuart on 5 July 1862 in a letter printed as Document 222 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was then running the British legation in Washington for the absent Lord Lyons.

The Fourth of July had just passed in a capital anxious about the war in Virginia. Stuart reported home on that mood while answering Seward's stream of letters. Exchanges like this one kept the two governments talking through a summer when many in Europe expected the Union to fail. And some hoped to profit from it. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d322:
Document 322 is the second Dayton report dated 3 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent both reports to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Paired reports often split the formal from the personal: ministry business in one, court impressions in the other. Early September 1862 needed both kinds, since French policy was made in the emperor's circle. This letter's mate and the Seward letters around them let a reader rebuild the Paris legation's week in unusual fullness. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d422:
Horace J. Perry opened July 1862 with a report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 1 July. It stands as Document 422 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed diplomatic record.

Perry wrote as McClellan's campaign before Richmond was collapsing, news that would test Union credit in every European capital. Spain's ministers had to judge whether the rebellion might yet win and what that would mean for Cuba. A Madrid report in such a week told Seward how much ground the Union was losing or holding abroad. The letter sits inside the long Spanish file that runs through the whole 1862 volume.
frus-1862-d522:
At The Hague, James Shepherd Pike received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 October 1862. It is Document 522 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

October orders could at last use the autumn's facts: Antietam had stopped Lee, and emancipation was now the declared policy of the government. Seward's instructions spread both points to every post. At The Hague, where antislavery feeling ran strong, the emancipation order was welcome material for Pike's work. The dispatch belongs to the brighter October file, in which Washington's tone shifted from defense to quiet confidence for the first time since spring.
frus-1862-d622:
Jacob S. Haldeman wrote from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 April 1862. His report is Document 622 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Spring reports from Stockholm carried the season's improving American news into a friendly court and recorded its reception. Haldeman's post also touched the emigration then binding Sweden to the American Midwest. It bound them family by family. No other European file in the volume quite shares that human link. His April letter belongs to the quiet northern correspondence that balanced the volume's crisis files. It is proof of something easy to forget. Large stretches of the Union's foreign relations in 1862 were calm, correct, and even warm.
frus-1863p1-d22:
Charles Francis Adams opened the new year with this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 22 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, one of two he sent that day.

New Year's Day 1863 was the day the freedom edict took force at home. In London, Adams's work went on as before: watch the cabinet, weigh the press, guard the Union's cause. His pair of letters that day shows the post at full stretch. This one begins the 1863 run of the most read file in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d122:
On 16 March 1863, William H. Seward closed a four-letter day with this note to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 122 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of a batch often swept up what the rest had left: a late fact or a small order. Seward's fourth letter of the day sits in that place. The set it ends shows the London brief worked through in a single sitting, a habit Seward kept all spring. This letter is the tail of that work, plain and brief.
frus-1863p1-d222:
Reporting on 26 June 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 222 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d322:
On 13 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 322 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the month of the Trent affair, when the seizure of two Confederate envoys from a British ship nearly caused a war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d422: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 March 1863. It is document 422 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d522:
Document 522 in the volume is a letter of 21 May 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington.
frus-1863p1-d622:
William Stuart, the British chargé d'affaires in Washington wrote this official letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 23 September 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020022:
Karl Simin, Hua Wu, Lucy Lu, and co-workers probed a tumor-blocking protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. The protein, pRb, acts as a brake on cell growth. The team switched it off in mouse mammary cells and watched how tumors began and grew in different tissues.

Loss of the brake set off shared steps across tissue types that normally behave quite differently. That overlap is useful news. It suggests that cancers driven by pRb loss may share weak points, whatever organ they start in. The paper helps frame pRb as more than a single-gene story. It shows how one broken brake can start a common path toward cancer.
plos-pbio-0020422:
Cydney B. Nielsen, Brad Friedman, and Bruce Birren compared introns across fungi in PLOS Biology in 2004. Introns are the gap stretches cut out of gene messages before use. Species differ hugely in how many introns their genes hold, and the team traced gains and losses across fungal family trees.

Their count shows both processes at work, with loss common in some lines and gain in others. That two-way traffic revises the simpler view that genomes only shed introns over time. Knowing the true pattern helps read genome history from present-day genes. Fungi, with many sequenced species of varied intron counts, are the ideal test case for such bookkeeping.
plos-pone-0000122:
Tariq Maqbool, Cedric Soler, Teresa Jagla, and colleagues published this developmental biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. Working with the fruit fly Drosophila, they study a gene called ladybird. The gene helps shape the muscles of the fly's legs as the insect develops.

Ladybird belongs to a family of genes that is conserved, meaning similar versions exist across many animals. The authors trace what the gene does as leg muscles form. The same gene family works in other species. So the fly results offer clues about how muscles are patterned in animals more broadly, including in limbs.
plos-pone-0000222:
Christine C. Boucard, Johannes M. Hoogduin, Jeroen van der Grond, and colleagues published this brain imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Patients with retinal visual field defects have damage in the eye that leaves blind regions in their sight. Using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy in the occipital lobe, the brain's vision area, the authors measured its chemistry.

The title reports their finding: metabolite concentrations were normal despite the visual defects. That means the brain tissue itself was chemically intact even where sight was lost at the eye. The result helps doctors separate eye damage from brain damage when reading scans of such patients.
plos-pone-0000322:
Joseph Schacherer, Douglas M. Ruderfer, David Gresham, and colleagues published this yeast genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lab strains of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae are used worldwide as if they were all the same. The authors analyze variation across the whole genome in commonly used strains and show how much they actually differ.

Small genetic differences between strains can change lab results. A variation catalogue lets researchers pick strains knowingly and interpret old results with care. The paper is a reference point for the yeast community and a warning for any field built on a model organism.
plos-pone-0000422:
Tae Won Kim, John H. Christy, and Jae C. Choe described a mating signal that doubles as a safety device, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In the animal they studied, females prefer a particular sexual signal from males. The title states their further claim: that preference keeps females safe.

A preference can persist for more than one reason. It picks good mates, but it also protects the chooser. It may steer her toward signals that reveal a safe situation. Studies like this complicate the usual story of sexual selection, where showy signals are assumed to cost the female time or risk. Here, following her preference is the safer move.
plos-pone-0000522:
Johannes Bergsten and Kelly B. Miller reconstructed the family tree of diving beetles and found a battle of the sexes written in it, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Male diving beetles have gripping suckers; females of some species have rough backs that resist grip. The beetle phylogeny revealed a coevolutionary arms race between the sexes.

An arms race means each sex's adaptation provokes the other's counter-adaptation over generations. A phylogeny lets researchers order the changes in time and test whether the traits really escalated together. Diving beetles give an unusually clear example because the structures are physical and the tree is well resolved.
plos-pone-0000622:
Rudi Alberts, Peter Terpstra, Yang Li and colleagues sounded a warning for gene-mapping studies in PLOS ONE in 2007. Researchers map eQTLs, places in the genome linked to how strongly a gene is expressed. Local eQTLs, where the linked place is the gene itself, look like the most direct and promising leads.

The authors argue that many of those local hits are false. Ordinary sequence differences between individuals, called polymorphisms, can fool the measurement and fake a link. Their title states the finding bluntly: sequence polymorphisms cause many false cis eQTLs. Anyone trusting published eQTL maps needs to reckon with this source of error.
plos-pone-0000722:
Majid Eshaghi, R. Krishna M. Karuturi, Juntao Li and colleagues profiled when and how well DNA copies itself in fission yeast. In S. pombe, replication starts at many origins, sites rich in A-T sequences, firing at various times during S-phase. Genome-wide studies had focused on replication timing and where origins sit, less on how efficiently each origin fires.

Their global profiling adds efficiency to the map. The title reports a surprise: efficient replication and firing occur late during S-phase. Late was often read as sloppy or secondary. Showing late firing as efficient rewrites part of how the copying schedule is understood, with lessons for larger genomes too.
plos-pone-0000822:
Tang Chi Thuong and co-authors looked into a grave outbreak of staph infections in children who had just been vaccinated. The germ was community-acquired MRSA, a form of Staphylococcus aureus that resists a key drug. Such infections were on the rise around the world at the time. The team ran a field study after bad events were reported at an out-patient clinic.

The germs carried a toxin gene called Panton-Valentine leukocidin, which is linked to severe disease. An outbreak after shots demands care: was the vaccine at fault, the clinic's hygiene, or mere chance? The report, in PLOS ONE in 2007, works through that proof. Clear field work of this kind keeps vaccine programs both safe and trusted.
plos-pone-0000922:
Jeffrey Roizen, Christina Luedke, Erik Herzog and colleagues examined oxytocin's role in the daily timing of birth, in PLOS ONE in 2007. What sets the clock for labor is still only partly known. The answer matters for care of births that come too early, too late or stall.

Oxytocin is the hormone that drives contractions, so the team tested whether it also carries a time of day signal for birth. Many births cluster at certain hours, hinting at a body clock at work. Tying that rhythm to a known hormone would give doctors a clearer picture of normal labor. It could also flag when timing, not strength, is the problem.
plos-pone-0001022:
Claudia Acquisti, George Poste, David Curtiss and colleagues questioned a popular reading of missing DNA words, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Nullomers are short DNA sequences that never appear in a species' genome. Many had assumed their absence is the signature of natural selection removing harmful sequences.

If true, nullomers could point to drug targets and other useful sites. The authors ask whether selection is really the explanation, or whether chance and mutation patterns suffice. Their title frames the doubt plainly. The paper is a check on a tempting inference: an absent pattern is not, by itself, proof that selection banned it.
plos-pone-0001122:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a cancer of the upper throat that is closely tied to Epstein-Barr virus and is especially common in southern China. Jiang Li and colleagues investigated the immune side of this cancer in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They asked whether the body's virus-specific defenses fail in people with the tumor.

The team assessed the look and function of T cells, immune cells meant to attack virus-infected cells, both in the blood and inside tumors. Their title reports functional inactivation of the Epstein-Barr virus-specific T cells. That failure could help explain how the tumor survives, and it shapes ideas for immune-based treatment.
plos-pone-0001222:
Autoimmune diseases arise when the gene networks controlling T-cell activation go wrong. Ricardo Palacios and colleagues modeled that network in humans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Understanding complex diseases, they argue, benefits from recognizing the properties of the gene networks that control biological functions.

From their network analysis of human T-cell activation, the authors identify Jagged1 as a therapeutic target for autoimmune diseases. Jagged1 is a ligand in the Notch pathway, which helps govern immune cell behavior. A network approach can surface targets that single-gene studies miss, because it looks at control points rather than individual actors.
plos-pone-0001322:
Glucosinolates are the pungent defense chemicals of cabbage-family plants, deterring herbivores and pathogens while attracting specialist insects. Ida Elken Sønderby and colleagues used a systems biology approach to find the genes controlling one class of them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Little was known about the genes that control these chemicals.

The authors identify three R2R3 MYB transcription factor genes with distinct and overlapping functions in regulation of aliphatic glucosinolates. Transcription factors are the switches of gene networks. Knowing the switches could let breeders tune these chemicals, which matter for pest resistance and human nutrition alike.
plos-pone-0001422:
William Freed and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on growing dopamine nerve cells from human embryo stem cells. Dopamine cells die in Parkinson's disease, so lab grown ones hold hope for repair. The team guided stem cells toward that fate, then sorted out the young nerve cells. They read the full gene pattern of the sorted cells.

The gene read out showed a strong signal from one stretch of chromosome 11. They also set the pattern side by side with that of real dopamine nerve cells. Close match would back the lab cells as a sound model. The data guide both graft work and drug screens for Parkinson's.
plos-pone-0001522:
Liya Wassie and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on TB patients in Ethiopia and their close contacts. A signal called IL-4 had been tied to TB, but its role stayed in dispute. The team had prior data from patients, contacts, and healthy controls in one cohort. Here they tracked signal gene levels over time in blood cells.

Signal levels moved in step with how patients' health changed. Contacts showed their own pattern as time passed. A blood mark that tracks disease state could help clinics judge who needs care most. It could also flag contacts who are sliding toward illness before signs show.
plos-pone-0001622:
Kosuke Fujishima and co-authors asked an old question about the origin of transfer RNA in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Transfer RNA, or tRNA, carries amino acids to the cell's protein-making machinery. In one archaeal parasite, Nanoarchaeum equitans, scientists had found tRNA genes split into separate 5-prime and 3-prime halves.

That find raised a clear question: did the first tRNA start as one gene or as two halves that later joined? The team ran a broad family-tree study of tRNAs across 45 archaeal genomes to test the idea. The full text gives the sequence evidence, the trees they built, and their case that modern tRNAs grew out of joined ancestral halves. The work speaks to how core parts of the cell first came together.
plos-pone-0001722:
Mariëlle I. Gallegos Ruiz and co-authors combined gene copy data with gene activity data in lung cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Lung cancer kills about 1.2 million people a year worldwide, and the non-small cell form makes up 85 percent of cases. Better early diagnosis and treatment require knowing its molecular events.

By integrating gene dosage with expression, the team identified HSP90 as a potential drug target. Dosage is how many copies of each gene a tumor carries; expression is how active those genes are. The full text gives the tumor samples, the combined analysis, and the evidence for HSP90. Targets found by two data types at once are less likely to be noise, which is why this joining of methods matters.
plos-pone-0001822:
Paola Laiolo, Matthias Vögeli, David Serrano, and their co-authors tested whether bird song can forecast population survival in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Habitat fragmentation is growing worldwide, and those who protect wild birds need signs of whether populations will last. Learned behaviors, above all sound signals, might carry such signs.

The team explored whether song diversity predicts how long broken-up bird groups last. They report that it does, as the title states. The full text gives the groups tracked and the song measures. A mic survey is far cheaper than years of bird counts. A reliable song sign would be a practical tool for watching over wild populations.
plos-pone-0001922:
Xiaotu Ma, Aaron Tarone, and Wenyuan Li built a map of backup paths in yeast genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A synthetic lethal pair is two gene faults that are harmless alone but kill the cell together, which hints the genes back each other up. Such pairs have long been used to guess what a gene does.

The team went past single pairs. They compared the whole pattern of lethal partners for each gene, since genes with like patterns tend to share a path. From those patterns they charted compensatory paths, the detours a cell can take. Maps like this help predict drug targets in germs and cancer.
plos-pone-0002022:
Thea Egelhofer and co-authors found a new early job for a family of yeast proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The proteins, septins, group at the spot where a bud will emerge in budding yeast, during the G1 stage of the cell cycle. They were not thought to do much that matters at that early stage.

The team show that septins work in G1 pathways that shape the pattern of cell growth. When septins fail, growth goes awry before the bud even forms. An early role for septins rewrites a piece of the cell cycle map in a model organism used across biology.
plos-pone-0002122:
Slaven Erceg and co-authors described a lab method in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper for turning human embryonic stem cells into early nerve cells. Stem cells taken from embryos can copy the first steps of human growth in a dish. Cells made from them might one day help repair tissue, such as nerve tissue hurt by disease or injury.

The team grew the stem cells in a defined medium, a mix with known contents and no unknown animal products. Under those clean conditions the cells became neural precursors, early cells set to form parts of the nervous system. Work like this matters for both basic research and future cell-based treatments.
plos-pone-0002222:
Erbo Ying, Dan Li, Shaojun Guo, and co-authors described a simpler way to make glowing nanocrystals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CdTe nanocrystals shine brightly and can tag cells for imaging under a microscope. Older recipes used tellurium sources that spoil on contact with air, which made the crystals hard to prepare well.

The team used stable sodium tellurite instead and made high-quality crystals in water in a single pot. A coating of mercaptosuccinic acid made the crystals bright and suited to bio-imaging. Easier recipes for bright probes help more labs light up cells and tissues for study.
plos-pone-0002322:
Erwin Boutsma, Sonja Noback, and Maarten van Lohuizen found a hidden start signal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The signal sits inside the message of a chromatin protein. Ring1B belongs to the Polycomb group, proteins that orchestrate development, cell growth, and stem cell fate by reshaping local chromatin. Ring1B is the enzyme that tags histone H2A with a single ubiquitin mark, a key silencing step.

The authors show the protein's own messenger RNA carries an IRES. That is an internal entry point letting protein building start mid-message, in its highly conserved head region. Such a backup start could keep Ring1B flowing when normal protein synthesis is throttled, for instance under stress.
plos-pone-0002422:
A research team led by Navis reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Marjon Navis, Diana Edo Matas, Andrea Rachinger, and others. Its subject is molecular Evolution of Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 upon Transmission between Human Leukocyte Antigen Disparate Donor-Recipient Pairs.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002522:
Work from Molokhia and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Mariam Molokhia, Paul McKeigue, Vasa Curcin, and others. Its subject is statin Induced Myopathy and Myalgia: Time Trend Analysis and Comparison of Risk Associated with Statin Class from 1991–2006. Statins are widely used as a cholesterol lowering medication, reduce cardiovascular death and morbidity in high risk patients.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002622:
Ralf Dressel led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the tumorigenicity of mouse embryonic stem cells and in vitro differentiated neuronal cells is controlled by the recipients' immune response. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ralf Dressel, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Embryonic stem (ES) cells have the potential to differentiate into all cell types and are considered as a valuable source of cells for transplantation. The summary also notes a further point. A critical issue, however, is the risk of teratoma formation after transplantation. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002722:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Yen-Chun Liu and colleagues addresses global regulation of nucleotide biosynthetic genes by c-Myc. The catalog record names Yen-Chun Liu first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The c-Myc transcription factor is a master regulator and integrates cell proliferation, cell growth and metabolism through activating thousands of target genes. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002822:
Francesca R. Dani led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was exploring proteins in anopheles gambiae male and female antennae through MALDI mass spectrometry profiling. Authorship is credited in the record to Francesca R. Dani and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. MALDI profiling and imaging mass spectrometry (IMS) are novel techniques for direct analysis of peptides and small proteins in biological tissues. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002922:
Martin Hoffmann, Hannah Chang, Sui Huang and co-authors modeled noise in stem cell populations in 2008. A stem cell must either stay a stem cell or mature into a specialist cell, and its surroundings tip that balance. Switching between states was long pictured as a move between stable states of a gene network.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors focus on stochastic fluctuations, random noise in molecule counts, as a driver of that switching. Their model covers stem and progenitor populations together. The view helps explain why sister cells with the same genes can take different paths.
plos-pone-0003022:
Caroline Blais, Rachael Jack, Christoph Scheepers and co-authors showed in 2008 that culture shapes how people look at faces. Face processing was long thought uniform across humans. Since 1965, eye movement studies had consistently found a triangular scan over eyes and mouth, suggesting a universal pattern.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team reports that viewing pattern is not universal after all. Culture shapes the strategy used to read a face. That finding changes cross-cultural psychology and design alike, from interviews to face software trained on narrow samples. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003122:
Kobby Essien, Sridhar Hannenhalli and Christian J. Stoeckert offer this 2008 PLOS ONE computer-based study of malaria parasites. Species of Plasmodium differ in clear ways, such as which hosts they choose and which cell types they prefer to invade. The authors argue that part of the reason for these traits lies in limits placed on gene activity and on coding and noncoding parts of the genome.

Using computation, they compare those limits across parasites with unlike traits. The study gives readers a way to link DNA patterns to the varied behaviour of malaria parasites. It may help explain why species that cause the same disease still act so differently.
plos-pone-0003222: Hironobu Fukami and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on the family history of stony corals. The title states its dual claim from mitochondrial and nuclear genes: stony corals stem from one common ancestor, but most named coral families do not. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no species or methods are added here.
plos-pone-0003322:
Norihiro Yumoto, Shuji Wakatsuki, Tomohiro Kurisaki and colleagues study proteins at the nerve-muscle junction in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Development of the neuromuscular junction starts with the forming of special postsynaptic zones in the central zones of muscles. Motor nerve terminals then arrive opposite the postsynaptic regions. The parts on both sides are then held firm.

The authors report Meltrin beta, or ADAM19, works with EphA4 in developing neural cells. It takes part in forming the neuromuscular junction. Readers learn of a new partnership in building the contact that lets nerves move muscle. Faults at this junction lie behind several muscle disorders present at birth.
plos-pone-0007422:
Olivier Masson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on LRP1, a receptor protein that sits on the surface of cells. LRP1 was already known for its role in how the body handles fats. The team asked a different question: what does LRP1 do while new fat cells are being made?

They found LRP1 present at high levels in mouse precursor cells on their way to becoming fat cells. Levels were also raised in the fatty tissue of obese mice and obese people. That pattern marks LRP1 as an active driver of fat cell formation rather than a bystander. The results name a possible target for future obesity research.
plos-pone-0007522:
Kyle McQuisten and Andrew Peek published a comparison study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on designing small interfering RNAs. These short RNA pieces can silence a chosen gene inside cells. Not every design works equally well, though. Machine learning tools promise to predict which ones will succeed. The authors pitted three approaches against each other: artificial neural networks, general linear models, and support vector machines.

Each method was tested on how well it predicted effective siRNAs. The head-to-head comparison also weighed the feature sets fed into the models. For researchers, the value is practical guidance. Choosing the right predictor means fewer wasted experiments on designs that fail. The study turns a crowded field of algorithms into clearer advice for anyone building gene-silencing tools.
plos-pone-0007622:
Hiromasa Tanaka and Tau-Mu Yi published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on mapping the wiring of cell signaling networks. A core goal of systems biology is to redraw those arrow diagrams completely. Genetic epistasis, comparing mutants, is a classic tool for ordering a pathway's parts. The authors present a strategy they call Alternative Inputs. It probes one network through several different entry signals.

Feeding a circuit different starting signals reveals the order of its components from new angles. Each input lights the network in a different pattern. Combined, the patterns pin down who acts upstream of whom. A systematic reverse-engineering method serves anyone facing an unmapped pathway. The study is a piece of strategy: how to interrogate a black box until it confesses its wiring.
plos-pone-0007722:
Maria Miragaia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It surveys a mobile piece of DNA in a common skin bacterium. The bacterium is Staphylococcus epidermidis, usually harmless on human skin. The DNA element, called ACME, carries genes for using arginine.

Mobile elements can hop between bacteria and spread new traits. The authors mapped how varied ACME is across many strains of this species. That diversity hints at how often the element moves and spreads. Tracking such elements matters because they can also carry traits that help bacteria resist treatment.
plos-pone-0007822:
Didier Delignieres and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It models how people tap along with a beat. Tapping in sync with a metronome is a basic timing skill. Tapping in syncopation, landing between beats, is harder.

In syncopation, the timing errors show stronger long-range patterns over time. The authors extend a classic linear phase correction model to explain that rise. Their model ties the patterns to how people fix small timing errors. The work helps scientists understand the brain's clock. It also speaks to music performance and rhythm disorders.
plos-pone-0007922:
Anna Ghelli and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how a person's mitochondrial background can raise the stakes of a toxin. Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy is an inherited blinding disease. It comes from point mutations in mitochondrial genes for complex I.

Many mutation carriers never lose vision, a puzzle called incomplete penetrance. The authors studied cells carrying haplogroup J, a common mitochondrial background. Those cells were more sensitive to a toxic compound, 2,5-hexanedione. The result shows how background DNA and environment jointly decide risk. It may help counsel carriers about exposures to avoid.
plos-pone-0008022:
Natacha Protopopoff and colleagues ranked what drives malaria in Africa's highlands for PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria is returning to high ground where people have little built-in defense, so outbreaks there can kill many. Control budgets are thin, so each measure must count.

The team scored the risk factors, from climate and land use to housing and care access, by their true weight. A ranked list lets programs spend first where the gain is largest. Blanket efforts waste scarce funds; aimed efforts, the authors argue, can blunt deadly highland outbreaks.
plos-pone-0008122:
Yongsoo Kim and colleagues watched the adult mouse brain's stem cell nursery in PLOS ONE in 2009. One brain zone keeps making new nerve cells for life. Its stem and progenitor cells were thought to roam, since their offspring, young neurons, plainly travel far.

The parents, it turns out, stay put. The team also found that a growth receptor holds back the young neurons' travel when it acts. A nursery with still parents and roaming young is a tidy design, and knowing it helps efforts to coax the brain to repair itself.
plos-pone-0008222:
Igor V. Bondar and colleagues studied visual neurons in monkeys in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Many neurons in the temporal lobe respond only to certain complex patterns. Faces and objects are classic examples of such stimuli. This selectivity is thought to arise through experience. Whether it stays stable over long periods was an open question.

The team recorded pattern-selective responses in monkey temporal lobe neurons over time. Long-term stability would mean visual memories can rely on fixed cell responses. Instability would imply the visual system keeps reshaping itself. Their measurements speak to how the brain stores what things look like.
plos-pone-0008322:
Işin Çakir and colleagues studied appetite control in the brain in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Sirt1 is a conserved enzyme involved in many processes in cells. It affects differentiation, cell death, metabolism, and aging. It depends on NAD+, a molecule tied to energy state. The team investigated Sirt1's role in the hypothalamus, the brain's energy balance center.

Using a rodent model, they showed hypothalamic Sirt1 regulates food intake. A brain enzyme linking energy signals to eating is a notable finding. It could point to new approaches for obesity. It also deepens understanding of how the brain senses fuel.
plos-pone-0008422:
Lance B. Price and colleagues studied circumcision and microbes in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. Circumcision is associated with large reductions in HIV and other infections among men. Female partners also show reduced bacterial vaginosis. The mechanisms behind these benefits were partly unclear. The team assessed the penis microbiome before and after circumcision.

They sampled the coronal sulcus of twelve HIV-negative Ugandan men. Circumcision changed the mix of bacteria living on the penis. Altered microbiota could explain part of the protection observed. The study adds biology to a major public health intervention.
plos-pone-0008522:
Sanjai Sinha and co-authors study prescribing for heart failure in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Beta-blockers reduce deaths in patients with systolic heart failure. Yet primary care doctors prescribe them at low rates. The team compare what doctors say they prescribe with what they actually prescribe. They also look for physician traits that predict prescribing. Data cover heart failure patients in primary care practice.

Self-reported and actual prescribing do not always match. Certain physician characteristics predict higher actual prescription rates. Closing the gap could save lives, since the benefit is well proven. The study points to which doctors may need support or prompts to prescribe.
plos-pone-0008622:
Marcel Adam Just and co-authors propose a theory of noun meaning in the brain in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their article describes a set of biologically driven semantic dimensions. Those dimensions underlie the neural representation of concrete nouns. In other words, brain codes for objects rest on basic sensory and motor features. The team demonstrate how the resulting theory can identify simple thoughts. They do so through fMRI patterns recorded while people think of nouns.

A model built on those dimensions predicts brain activation for new nouns. It can even identify which noun a person is thinking of. Such a neurosemantic theory links word meaning to brain biology. It advances efforts to read semantic content from brain scans.
plos-pone-0008722:
Ivan Tancevski, Egon Demetz, Philipp Eller, and colleagues tested a thyroid-like drug aimed only at the liver. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compound, T-0681, mimics thyroid hormone in liver tissue. Such drugs can raise receptors that pull cholesterol from the blood. A liver-only action might spare the heart from thyroid side effects.

The team measured reverse cholesterol transport, the path that carries cholesterol out for disposal. They also watched artery plaque build-up in treated mice. Better transport paired with slower plaque growth would support the approach. The study weighs promise against the risks of thyroid mimicry.
plos-pone-0008822:
David Simpson, Edward Kabyemela, Atis Muehlenbachs, and colleagues tied a blood protein to severe anemia in pregnancy malaria. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Placental malaria kills about ten thousand mothers yearly in Africa. First-time mothers face the greatest risk. Inflammatory signals like TNF-alpha were already linked to the anemia. The team measured apolipoprotein A1, a fat-carrying protein, in exposed women.

Higher A1 levels tracked with severe anemia in first pregnancies. The protein may mark the inflammatory state driving red cell loss. A blood marker could flag mothers needing urgent care. Protecting first pregnancies remains a malaria priority.
plos-pone-0008922:
Zhuoshun Yang, Biao Zhang, Dapeng Li, and colleagues showed mast cells recruiting immune suppressors inside liver tumors. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors often grow amid chronic inflammation that should attack them. Instead, inflammation and immune suppression become braided together. Mast cells pile up in this liver cancer model and worsen matters. How they tilt the tumor's immune balance was the question.

Mast cells mobilized two suppressor groups: myeloid-derived suppressor cells and regulatory T cells. The IL-17 pathway carried the mobilizing signal. Suppressors then shielded the tumor from attack. Breaking the mast cell signal could unshield liver tumors for therapy.
plos-pone-0009022:
Francisco Ortega and co-authors listed the tiny RNA regulators in human belly fat, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that fine-tune gene activity. Some are tied to body fat and differ between fat depots. No profile yet existed for fat cells as they mature, the team noted.

They profiled microRNAs in human under-skin fat tissue. They also followed the profile as precursor cells became fat cells. Certain microRNAs rose or fell in step with that change. The catalogue points to which tiny RNAs may steer weight gain or loss.
plos-pone-0009122:
Michèl Schummer and co-authors compared breast tumours with healthy breast tissue to find new warning proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early detection saves lives in breast cancer, above all for poor-outcome cases. Good markers for predicting a patient's course are still scarce. The study drew on two carefully characterised sets of tissue.

One set contrasted patients whose outcomes were good with those whose were poor. The other set came from healthy women and served as the control. Proteins that differed across the sets became candidate markers for follow-up. Markers that flag aggressive cancer early could change screening and care.
plos-pone-0009222:
Vibha Gupta and colleagues published this structural biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines an enzyme from the tuberculosis bacterium, a germ wrapped in a fatty coat. The enzyme, biotin protein ligase, has flexible loops near the spot where it grabs its target. In water those loops are disordered, waving around without a fixed shape.

The team studied what happens when the water is removed. Drying locked the loose loops into ordered, active shapes. That switch shows how the enzyme may fold only when conditions are right. Understanding such shape changes in a tuberculosis enzyme can guide the design of new drugs against the disease.
plos-pone-0009322:
Laura Gosoniu, Andre Mia Veta, and Penelope Vounatsou published this malaria mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Angola runs national surveys that sample malaria indicators across the country. Survey points are sparse, but health planners need estimates everywhere. The space between sample points must be filled in with care.

The authors applied Bayesian geostatistical modeling to the Angolan survey data. Their model blends the survey results with geography to predict risk in unsampled places. It also states how uncertain each prediction is. Such maps help target bed nets, spraying, and clinics where malaria is truly worst, not just where it was measured.
plos-pone-0011422:
Kristen Taylor and co-authors reported in 2010 that high blood sugar and a chronic inflammation signal together disable a class of guard cells. Gamma-delta T cells patrol body surfaces and respond fast to germs, and people with obesity and metabolic disease suffer more infections. The team used mouse models to test what dulls these guards.

Mice with high blood sugar and lasting exposure to the inflammation signal TNF-alpha had fewer gamma-delta T cells, and the remaining cells responded weakly. Neither insult alone told the full story; the double hit did the damage. The result helps explain the infection risk that travels with diabetes and obesity. It also suggests that controlling sugar and inflammation together, not either one alone, may be needed to restore this first line of defense.
plos-pone-0011522:
Stephanie Topp and co-authors tested in 2010 whether HIV treatment can be folded into ordinary clinics in Lusaka, Zambia. Antiretroviral therapy was often delivered in separate, donor-funded programs, apart from the primary care that the same patients use for everything else. Separation strains both systems and stigmatizes patients, so the team studied the feasibility of integration at facility level.

Their work asked a practical question of staff, space, and patient flow: can the same nurses and rooms handle routine care and HIV treatment together? Feasibility evidence of this kind is what ministries need before changing national policy. If integration works, overstretched systems gain efficiency and patients gain one door instead of two. The study treats organization itself as a medical intervention, which in a strained health system it truly is.
plos-pone-0011622:
Ashley Sherrid and co-authors studied how tuberculosis bacteria handle low oxygen, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The TB bacillus can stop growing and lie dormant when oxygen runs low, as happens inside lung granulomas during infection. How the bacteria enter, hold and leave that dormant state is a major research focus.

The team characterised a gene regulator tied to the Clp protease, a protein-shredding system, and tracked the response when oxygen returns. Their findings expose controls the bacteria use to wake from dormancy. Those wake-up controls are attractive drug targets, since dormant TB is notoriously hard to kill.
plos-pone-0011722:
Christine Ward-Paige, Joanna Mills Flemming and Heike Lotze warned about a bias in reef fish surveys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Divers increasingly count fish visually underwater to assess populations and to judge whether protected areas work. Such censuses underpin many claims about natural reef communities.

The authors show that counts taken slowly, rather than as instant snapshots, systematically overestimate fish numbers. Fish wander into the survey area during a long count and get tallied extra. Protection plans built on inflated counts may therefore miss their mark, so survey methods need correcting.
plos-pone-0011822:
Jing Yan Tang and co-authors tested a plant compound that spurs new blood vessels, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vessel growth, called angiogenesis, plays a part in a wide range of body processes, and many diseases trace to its poor control. Radix Astragali is a Chinese herb used for heart and vessel ills, and it had been shown to hold vessel-linked gains.

Its compound calycosin spurred vessel growth in zebrafish and in human vessel cells, acting through estrogen receptors and the MAPK signal path. A natural agent that grows vessels could help wounds heal and injured tissue recover, where new blood supply lines are needed.
plos-pone-0011922:
John Schneider and colleagues surveyed in 2010 Indian truck drivers about two HIV prevention options still new at the time. Long-haul drivers face elevated HIV risk, and prevention plans often fail at the first step: whether people will accept them. The options were daily preventive medicine, called pre-exposure prophylaxis, and circumcision.

Using a staged behavior model, the team measured the drivers' initial commitment to each option, working with ninety drivers. Knowing whether the barrier is awareness, interest, or firm intent tells health workers where outreach will pay off. For a mobile population that clinics rarely keep in touch with, that first commitment is the foothold everything else depends on.
plos-pone-0012022:
Timothy Dickson and Charles Mitchell tested in 2010 how insects and fungi, alone and together, cut seed production in grassland plants. Herbivores and fungal pathogens each reduce plant fitness, and their joint effects may add up, cancel, or multiply. Few studies had measured those joint effects on seeds in wild, non-crop populations.

Excluding each enemy in turn across four common grassland species let the team separate the costs. Seeds are the currency of plant futures, so even modest cuts change which species dominate a meadow. The results help ecologists predict grassland change as insect and fungal communities shift with climate and land use.
plos-pone-0012122:
Alison McCormack, Sally Mak, Jaimie Henderson, and co-authors tested a gene-silencing treatment in monkeys for PLOS ONE in 2010. A brain protein called alpha-synuclein sits at the center of Parkinson's disease, and too much of it seems to add to its harm. Lowering the protein in the brain region that dies in Parkinson's could, in theory, slow the disease.

Showing that levels can be turned down safely in a large animal brain is a needed step before any human trial. plos-pone-0012422:

plos-pone-0012522:

People understand the world by linking events that influence each other, and groups aggregate many such links into collective memory — the shared story of what happened and what matters. The authors built a model in which linked event pairs spread and merge through social contact. Collective memory arose as a natural outcome of many small exchanges, not from any central editor. The model offers testable ideas about how communities come to remember the same past.

pmc-4170722:

Mendelian randomization uses genes as anchors. Since gene variants are set at conception, they act like a natural random trial of a lifelong exposure. If people with a variant also have more disease, that supports a real causal link. The method helps test whether factors like blood pressure or cholesterol truly cause illness.

plos-pone-0357022:
Samson Tashome Abashu leads a team of four auditing the paperwork behind HIV care in Jimma, Ethiopia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Treatment programs run on records; bad data means invisible failures. The team reviewed two hundred thirty-four patient files across five public facilities in mid 2022. They scored the resources available and the quality of the data itself. They also checked whether anyone actually used the information for decisions.

The three scores landed in the seventies, a middling verdict. Completeness was good, above ninety percent, and consistency acceptable. Timeliness was the wound, under half of reports arriving when due. Some facilities lacked the electronic record system, internet, or even printers. No staff in the testing service had been trained on data quality, and performance review meetings were not happening as scheduled. The authors say Jimma's HIV data are usable but fragile, held up by habit more than by systems.

plos-pone-0352922:
Romaric Jac led a team of eight authors studying capelin in Canada's Gulf of St. Lawrence, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Capelin are small forage fish that feed many larger species, so their movements matter to the whole food web. The team asked whether capelin stay faithful to home regions or disperse widely.

Jac's group read chemical traces in otoliths, the ear stones that record a fish's history in its layers. Those fingerprints reveal which fish are locals and which traveled in. The answer shapes how fisheries should be managed: local stocks need local protection, while wide-ranging fish need broader plans. plos-pone-0358122:
Max Y. Lu and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how interest in anesthesiology changes during medical school, using national data on American medical students who entered between 2014 and 2017. Women and sexual minority students are underrepresented in the specialty, and little was known about low-income trainees. The authors sorted students into four paths: never interested, gained interest, lost interest, or kept interest from entry to graduation.

Nearly all students, over nine in ten, were never interested, and only a small fraction kept the interest throughout. Women started out less interested than men, and women and sexual minority students were less likely to develop interest during school, even though those who began interested kept it at similar rates. Low-income students showed no clear differences. The specialty, they argue, loses trainees mainly by failing to spark interest early, especially among women, not by losing those already keen.
plos-pone-0357622:
Ying Shi, Yi Bao, and Chuanxiong Li published a 2026 systematic review in PLOS ONE on using musculoskeletal ultrasound to steer rehabilitation after rotator cuff repair. Shoulder rehab after tendon surgery usually advances by calendar, yet patients heal at different speeds and pushing early risks re-tear. Ultrasound watches the tendon and muscle directly. The reviewers searched three databases for studies linking ultrasound measures to rehab decisions, finding eleven.

Three measures dominated: shear wave velocity, a stiffness index, plus the muscle's cross-sectional area and echo brightness. Stiffness climbed steadily across the first year after surgery, giving a rough baseline trajectory for normal healing. An unusually high stiffness reading soon after surgery flagged higher re-tear risk and argued for slowing the program down. The evidence is early and thin, but it sketches how imaging could replace fixed timetables with healing-based progression, a shift trials should now test.
plos-pone-0357922:

The signals include the heart's electric trace, its sounds, its chest vibrations, and two pulse measures taken at the skin. Each method is well studied alone, yet side-by-side comparisons under one setup are rare, which makes combining them into one monitor hard.

Electric and pulse signals proved steady in shape and timing, while sound and vibration signals varied more with sensor placement and body differences. Each signal also carried its energy in a distinct pitch band, and delays against the electric trace matched known body timing. Charlier and colleagues publish the benchmarks to guide filter choices and multi-signal heart monitors.

One variant's mixed form raised risk clearly across several genetic models, while its double form looked protective in one model; the second variant showed no clear link. Patients carried more of the controller protein and less of the guard, with levels tracking gene type. Chowdhury and colleagues say the variant deserves study as a risk marker in South Asian women.
plos-pone-0356722:
