It then confirmed the recipe with patient samples. The team varied preservative dose, spinning steps, storage temperature and time, and thawing method. DNA yield and purity were scored throughout.

Untreated urine degraded within a day at room temperature. The winning protocol spins the urine first. It adds a modest dose of preservative to the liquid portion, and freezes deep for long storage. Gentler freezing failed after about two months. Quick thawing proved safe, while extra spinning after thawing cost DNA. Such groundwork matters because urine DNA tests promise painless cancer and transplant monitoring.
plos-pone-0356822:
Uxía Yáñez and colleagues analyzed more than three and a half thousand uterine samples from mares. They wanted to settle a practical question in horse breeding. When bacteria grow in a mare's uterus culture, does it signal real inflammation or harmless contamination? Their 2026 study paired culture results from two sampling methods, swabs and low-volume washes. Microscopic inflammation scores came from the same samples.

Any bacterial growth raised the odds of inflammation with both methods. Counterintuitively, wash samples growing a single species were more often inflamed than those growing three or more. The busier growth looked more like contamination. One streptococcus species was the standout culprit across methods. Pairing culture with cytology, the authors argue, keeps antibiotics for mares who actually need them.
plos-pone-0354822:
Sylvia Aponte-Hao and seven colleagues use province-wide health records to ask who still ends up severely ill with COVID-19 after vaccination, in this 2026 Alberta study. They followed more than two and a half million adults who completed at least a primary vaccination schedule, tracking hospitalizations and deaths tied to the virus. Only a small fraction, about two in a thousand, suffered a severe outcome.

Risk concentrated sharply. Older age carried much higher hazard. A heavy burden of other illnesses multiplied risk many times over, and conditions such as cardiovascular disease and dementia stood out individually. Men fared slightly worse than women. The patterns held among people who took additional booster doses. The authors say the findings can guide booster policy and early treatment toward the vaccinated groups who remain genuinely vulnerable.
plos-pone-0351822:
Hannah Potter and four colleagues refine a low-tech trick for restoring seagrass meadows in this 2026 experiment. Seagrass is vanishing worldwide, and seeds sown bare are often eaten or churned up before they can grow. Wrapping seeds of a common eelgrass in clay balls protects them, but the recipe matters. The team tested clay mixes and drying methods in tanks, placing balls on the sediment surface or burying them, then tracked how well balls held together and how seedlings emerged.

A clear trade-off appeared. Bare seeds and buried balls of one clay type produced the most seedlings and longest shoots, while dense balls rich in certain clays survived deployment best but suppressed emergence. A mix lacking loam performed worst on every measure. Even so, surface balls beat typical field germination, and the authors see a scalable tool pending open-water trials.
plos-pone-0355722:
Kristina Åhlund, Anette Johnsson, and Maria Rönnerhag review in 2026 what helps or blocks nurses and physiotherapists learning together in hospital wards. Their scoping review searched three databases and kept a small set of studies that covered both professions in adult hospital care. Learning together matters because each group must grasp the other's role to care well.

Friendly team habits, chances to get to know each other, and supportive organisation helped learning. Tight structures, strained contact between professions, and a closed ward culture held it back. The authors argue that lasting learning needs regular contact built into normal work, plus leaders who welcome joint work even as staff change.
plos-pone-0345722:
Zhicheng Tan, Shanlin Sun, and Guo Li present in 2026 a neural network for spotting tiny hot targets in infrared images, such as distant ships or vehicles. Such targets give weak signals and little texture, so they are easy to miss or confuse with background noise. Their network uses a retention style attention that links far apart parts of an image without blurring fine detail.

An added module joins space and frequency views to pass clear target features through the system. Tests on several public datasets beat leading methods and cut training time by nearly a third. Faster, sharper spotting helps watching traffic and coasts from a distance.
plos-pone-0354522:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 review, work out how much balance training is enough for older adults. Falls are a leading danger in old age, and training that sharpens the senses and muscles can rebuild balance. But trials vary wildly in dose, and more may not always mean better. The team pooled twenty-four trials with over a thousand participants and modeled dose as a curve.

Training clearly improved both moving balance, such as standing up and walking, and still balance, such as standing steady. For moving balance the dose curve bent: gains grew, then softened around a total of roughly a thousand minutes of training. Still balance showed no such dose pattern. Age also mattered: older participants gained less in moving balance, while their still balance gains held up. The authors urge prescribers to dose balance training like medicine, enough to work, not endlessly more.
plos-pone-0354022:
Han-Trong and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a noise filter that adjusts itself while it runs, for sensors whose noise keeps changing. Steady filters fail when interference drifts, and heavy filters are too slow for small devices. Their design stacks stages of a classic adaptive filter and decides on the fly how many stages to run and how fast each should learn.

A statistical test watches whether the cleaned signal still echoes the noise reference, and stops the chain when the echo is gone. Corrections handle signals that resemble themselves and changing loudness of noise. On simulated and real measured data, the method cut errors sharply against the classic single filter and ran several times faster than a fixed-threshold rival. The authors aim it at low-delay monitoring on cheap hardware, from factory floors to body sensors.
plos-pone-0354122:
Araya Tipsungnoen and six colleagues review more than a decade of catheter procedures that close a heart duct in children, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Thai hospital. The duct, which should seal after birth, sometimes stays open and is now usually plugged through a vein rather than by open surgery. Three hundred and forty-one patients treated between 2010 and 2023 were checked for difficult procedures and major problems.

Trouble arose in about one case in seven, though nobody died from the procedure. A wider duct, a longer duct, and a duct shape other than the usual cone each roughly tripled the odds of difficulty. Three devices slipped free and needed surgery. Anatomy, the authors argue, should guide how carefully each case is planned.
plos-pone-0351722:
Xiaolong Zhang and three colleagues study how elite sprinters and power athletes should schedule their competitions in an Olympic or World Championship year, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis. Their dataset holds nearly fifteen thousand athlete records from global championships between 1993 and 2019. Statistical clustering sorted athletes into three seasonal styles: those who focused almost entirely on the big event, those who raced often, and those who treated races as training.

The frequent racers performed best at the main event. Athletes using races as training gained by moving toward the frequent-racing style, while big-event specialists gained nothing by switching. The authors' message to coaches is that the fashionable peak-for-one-day calendar suits only some athletes.
plos-pone-0353622:
Calahorro and colleagues built a free computer tool in 2026 to screen chemicals that may disturb hormones in fish. Testing every chemical on every kind of fish in the lab would take far too long. Their tool predicts how strongly a chemical will grip the hormone sensor proteins that start many toxic effects.

The tool screened the sensors of more than one hundred kinds of fish against natural and man-made steroid drugs. One fish group showed sensors that grip the drugs tightly, marking them as more at risk. Follow-up cell tests confirmed two chemicals from a health research set could switch the sensor on, flagging them for closer safety checks.
plos-pone-0353122:
Confessor and colleagues surveyed Japanese gamers at risk of social withdrawal in a 2026 study. Nearly six hundred players reported their withdrawal risk and gaming tastes. People who withdraw from society might also avoid social play, or might find online contact safer than face-to-face life.

Higher withdrawal risk tied to weaker interest in achievement and challenge-driven play. Other social tastes varied by gamer personality type. Games meant as bridges back to social life must match those tastes, or they may push players further away. The findings caution designers that one social game formula will not fit all withdrawn players.
plos-pone-0352422:
Jing Wang and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One cell study on kidney damage caused by the iodine contrast dye used in medical imaging. The work centers on a mitochondrial housekeeping protein called ClpP. Human kidney cells exposed to the dye in culture lost viability, their mitochondria fragmented, and programmed cell death rose; gene sequencing showed the dye switched on ClpP and related machinery.

When the team knocked ClpP down, the cells fared better: mitochondrial shape and energy held up more, a key fusion protein recovered, and fewer cells died. The authors suggest that restraining this protein softens contrast injury, at least in a dish, and nominate it as a target worth testing in animal models of contrast-related kidney damage.
plos-pone-0351422:
Hitomi Hagawa and four colleagues test a corn-derived ingredient that may help skin defend itself. Their 2026 study works with human skin cells called keratinocytes. Pollution and ultraviolet light bombard skin with oxidative stress. That stress speeds ageing and disorders. The ingredient is hydrolysed corn starch containing a sugar chain named maltotetraose. The team asked whether it switches on the cells' own antioxidant machinery, governed by a protein called NRF2.

Gene screening gave the first answer. Treated cells turned up several antioxidant genes, including three classic NRF2 targets. Protein tests confirmed more NRF2, and showed it moving into the cell nucleus where it works. Under deliberate oxidative attack, treated cells carried lower levels of harmful reactive oxygen. The effect runs through the skin's built-in defence pathway, not through a surface coating. Cosmetic formulators gain a food-derived candidate for protective skin products.
plos-pone-0351922:
Linh Nguyen and Tham Vo redesign how neural networks learn from social graphs. Their 2026 paper builds a framework called DAGRL. Standard graph networks pass messages between neighbours. That captures local closeness well. It smears together signals that live at different scales, though. Friend-of-friend patterns, community structure, and whole-network shape all blur into one average. The authors argue that local and global information deserve separate handling before they meet.

Dual attention mechanisms do the separating. One attends to fine-grained local interactions. The other reads the graph's global organisation. Their outputs combine into richer node representations. The framework is aimed at the usual proving grounds: classifying nodes, clustering communities, and inferring relationships. For analysts of online networks, cleaner separation of scales could mean spotting both tight cliques and the slow tides moving an entire platform.
plos-pone-0352322:
Yu Weng tracks the keystrokes of translators racing the clock. The 2026 study recruited sixty-five Chinese-to-English translators: thirty-five novices and thirty seasoned professionals. Each translated comparable texts under three deadlines: short, standard, and unlimited. Software logged every pause, burst, and revision. Analysis worked at two levels, from micro-pauses up to how whole sessions were organised. The question was how experience changes the rhythm of work under pressure.

Looser deadlines helped everyone. Text came in longer, steadier segments, with more immediate self-correction. Beyond that, the groups split. Experienced translators kept stable rhythms in every condition. They separated drafting from revision and spent time orienting first and polishing last. Novices blended everything reactively. Curiously, a moderate deadline made novices work most like experts. Unlimited time, which should have freed them, went unexploited. Training programmes can teach the expert cadence deliberately, rather than hoping years supply it.
plos-pone-0352022:
Nuhad Dumit and colleagues surveyed hospital nurses caring for Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Jordan, asking how the work was wearing on their own bodies and minds. About a thousand nurses answered in Lebanon and two thousand in Jordan. The survey covered back pain, general weakness, and emotional exhaustion alongside hours, workload, and workplace strain.

Strong back pain troubled more than six in ten nurses in both countries. General weakness was reported by nearly six in ten in Lebanon and more than seven in ten in Jordan. Emotional exhaustion also ran high, and higher in Jordan. Age, gender, and working hours were among the factors tied to the outcomes. Nurses holding up refugee care are themselves a strained workforce, and the numbers argue their health belongs on the response agenda.
plos-pone-0341522:
Yency Forero and colleagues asked whether repeat blood tests beat a single reading for judging lung spots. The marker they tracked is a protein fragment shed by lung tumors. Doctors usually read it once. The team instead followed it over time in over a hundred people with lung nodules. The patients came from a Vanderbilt tissue bank. The logic borrows from repeat prostate testing, where trends guide care.

At the first reading, cancer patients already ran higher than benign cases. Over time, the average paths did not split cleanly. But cancer cases swung more from visit to visit. The size of that swing separated the groups with very few false alarms. A jumpy trend may tell doctors more than any single value can.
plos-pone-0352122:
Abdi Negasa and colleagues modeled the value of a cheap breathing device for young children in Ethiopia. The device is called bubble CPAP. It pushes air gently to keep small lungs open. It can be built locally, unlike costly imported machines. The team compared it with standard low-flow oxygen in general hospitals. Their model counted deaths and healthy years gained.

For every ten thousand children with severe pneumonia and low blood oxygen, the device saved about thirty-one more lives. The cost per healthy year gained sat far below the usual limits for Ethiopia. Every check on the model gave the same answer. The authors urge wider use of the locally built device.
plos-pone-0351222:
Ebrahim Zarepour Nasirabadi and colleagues surveyed about seven hundred fifty parents of toddlers in Tabriz, Iran, about child car seats: what they know, own, and actually use. Road injuries kill children worldwide, and Iran's seat use lags its car ownership. Questionnaires at nineteen public health centers probed awareness, trust, cultural attitudes, and practical barriers.

The knowledge-behavior gap is stark. Nearly all families owned a car and most knew the age and weight rules, yet under half owned a seat, and over half of those rarely or never used it. Knowing how to install one correctly was the weakest knowledge point. Cultural and cost barriers filled out the picture. Campaigns that only teach rules will miss, the authors imply: the binding constraints are price, habit, and the hands-on skill of fitting the seat.
plos-pone-0349122:
A bulging aorta can be repaired from inside the vessel. The fix avoids open surgery. Late leaks still threaten some patients, though. Hong-Jae Choi and colleagues built a model to forecast long-term survival. They studied more than twelve thousand repair patients. Treatment years ran from 2002 to 2019.

Five learning methods fed into one stacked model. Thirty-four patient variables went into the forecasts. The stack ranked risk better than any single method. It won at both one month and one year. Importance charts show which traits drive each forecast. Surgeons can use the output in counseling. Patients hear a personal outlook, not a generic average.
plos-pone-0351622:
Lung adenocarcinoma, the most common lung cancer type, builds a neighborhood of immune cells that can help or hinder it. Jie Yao, Changshuai Zhou, and Liren Ding focused on an enzyme called KYNU inside macrophages, the immune system's cleanup cells, in this 2026 PLOS One data study.

Blending single-cell and bulk gene data from public atlases, they found the enzyme concentrated in macrophages and monocytes. Macrophages carrying it switched on genes for showing tumor pieces to other immune cells, and signaled more with B and T cells. Tumors rich in such macrophages behaved differently on immune measures. The authors call the analysis exploratory, a map for experiments rather than settled biology.
plos-pone-0350222:
Muhammad Tafazzal Hossain and colleagues tested shop bought cheese in Sylhet, Bangladesh, for a germ that resists common drugs. Over six months they gathered one hundred and twenty cheeses from twelve brands. In the lab they counted the germ, checked which drugs still worked, and searched for genes that make toxins.

About two thirds of samples carried the germ, often above safe limits, and about three in ten carried the drug resistant form. All resistant samples beat several widely used drugs. Many also carried toxin genes that can cause food poisoning and skin harm. The authors warn that everyday cheese can carry a real health risk when hygiene and cold storage fail.
plos-pone-0331722:
Candicia M Kotra and Lisa L Gezon looked at trade in khat, a leaf people chew for its lift, in northern Madagascar. Around Diego-Suarez they spoke with city managers and growers, watched sales points, and asked twenty sellers to keep daily diaries of earnings and costs. They set khat earnings beside earnings from selling vegetables.

Khat selling paid more than vegetable selling, even though prices swung with the seasons. Sellers with family ties to khat farms earned the most by far. Khat also brings jobs and town taxes that pay for local services and building work. Vegetables still draw sellers who lack farm family links. The study shows a drug crop quietly holding up much of the local economy.
plos-pone-0349622:
Andrea Levy and Ursula Rothlisberger tested two fast computer tools that predict where metal based drugs will bind on proteins. Such drugs show promise against cancer, yet finding their grip points is hard. Both tools were trained only on zinc sites, a narrow start. The test asked whether they could still spot true binding sites for other metal drugs on known protein shapes.

For every protein tried, at least one true site was found by the tools. Results wobbled when protein side chains sat in odd poses, a known weakness. The authors propose a pipeline: cheap predictors flag likely hot spots first, then costlier physics methods refine the shortlist. Drug hunters could save large computing bills that way.
plos-pone-0351322:
Correction notice: Christina M Ferreira and colleagues correct their study that used tiny worms to judge how harmful closely related Salmonella Newport strains from the environment can be. One author name was misspelled, two main figures were swapped, and species names needed italic styling in places. Corrected figures are supplied with this notice.

Readers should use the corrected author spelling, Arjumand Ghazi, and match each figure image to its caption in the new order. Figure captions themselves were already in the right order. The worm survival results and strain comparisons stand as captioned once the images are placed correctly. Anyone citing or reusing the figures should take them from the corrected version.
plos-pone-0351122:
Gabriele Bertotti and colleagues tested whether eating more polyphenols, plant compounds in fruit, vegetables, tea, and cocoa, links with lower pain sensitivity in migraine patients. Seventy two adults with confirmed migraine kept three day food records and took pressure pain tests on head and other sites, plus disability and stress surveys.

Higher intake went with higher pressure pain thresholds at two head muscles and lower disability scores. Adjusted models kept those links. People with longer migraine history also ate more polyphenols, perhaps learning by trial what helps. A snapshot cannot prove diet eases migraine, but the pattern supports trials of polyphenol rich diets for pain control.
plos-pone-0350822:
Adam P Burch, M Kristen Hall, and Ruth A Schwalbe studied a sugar tagging enzyme in neuroblastoma, a childhood nerve cancer. The enzyme adds a branch that can block further sugar chain growth, and it has a reputation for slowing tumours. Human cancer cells with the enzyme gene removed were compared with normal cells, and rat cancer cells with extra enzyme were also tested.

Removing the enzyme sped cell growth, movement, clumping, and invasion into surroundings. Tagged sugars of the blocked type nearly vanished, while other sugar types rose. Restoring the gene reversed the changes, and extra enzyme in rat cells calmed movement and invasion. Low enzyme activity marks more aggressive disease in this cancer model.
plos-pone-0350922:
Patricia Quintero-Rincon, Karina Caballero-Gallardo, and Oscar Florez-Acosta built dissolving microneedle patches from chitosan, a shell derived material, loaded with tequila agave root extract. Tiny needles that melt into skin promise painless delivery. Chemical profiling, shape and heat tests, enzyme assays, and skin and melanoma cell tests compared two extract loadings.

Rosmarinic acid led the extracts rich chemistry. The lower loading kept needle tips sharp, while the higher loading roughened surfaces and bent tips. Patches kept most antioxidant and skin enzyme effects of the extract, stayed gentle on normal skin cells, and killed melanoma cells in a dose linked way. Loading balance decides whether beauty or drug patches from agave can work.
plos-pone-0347922:
Xiaoxue Sherry Gao and Rong Rong studied a snag in survey science. How can you pay people to state their health beliefs with care? Pay schemes need a truth that can be checked. Health outcomes are private, and they unfold slowly. Worse, people could bet against their own health to win either way. The pair found a way around both traps.

They asked people about close peers, not about themselves. A first survey got real health facts from peers much like the group. Those facts set the pay in the main task. Beliefs about peers then lined up well with each person's own past health. The pair say peer beliefs can stand in for self-beliefs. Health researchers can use the trick.
plos-pone-0350122:
Carlotta Gualco, Maria Grazia Grasso, Giorgia Presicce, and co-authors mapped the world's research on helping people with multiple sclerosis get into work, stay in work, or return after absence. The disease often strikes in prime working years, and job support services exist but are little studied. Their 2026 scoping review searched seven databases and included twenty-eight studies describing distinct programs, appearing from the mid-nineteen-nineties through 2025, largely in Western nations.

Most programs combined several elements: rehabilitation, education, and workplace adjustments. Patients valued personal, empathetic support, help managing symptoms, and legal advice, while logistics and health problems blocked participation. Studies have grown more experimental lately, with feasibility trials multiplying. The authors judge the programs broadly feasible and call for stronger outcome evidence.
plos-pone-0349022:
Prakash Babu Kodali and Maya Vijayaraghavan used two rounds of India's big national family health survey to ask how often doctors and other health workers tell men who smoke to quit. They focused on men who smoked cigarettes or bidis and had seen a health worker in the past year. They compared survey rounds from the middle of the last decade with the most recent one.

Advice to quit rose slightly between the rounds, reaching a little over half of these men. Older men, heavier smokers, and men already diagnosed with a long-term illness were more likely to be advised. Men from Scheduled Tribe communities were notably less likely to hear the advice. The authors say a huge chance to help men quit is still being missed at routine visits.
plos-pone-0312222:
Abrham Shumbulo, Mihret Jemal, and Abraham Bosha ran a field trial at Wachemo University in southern Ethiopia to find the fertiliser mix that grows the most garlic. Ethiopian garlic yields are held back by tired soils and the lack of advice tuned to each area. Their plots combined five rates of a blended mineral fertiliser with four rates of chicken manure, repeated across blocks through one growing season.

The heaviest manure paired with a high-but-not-highest mineral dose won clearly, producing marketable bulbs more than ten times the unfertilised yield. It also brought the best dry matter and sweetness readings and the highest profit per hectare. Manure alone also lifted bulb quality. The authors recommend the winning combination to local growers, while noting the mix was tuned on one demonstration field and season.
plos-pone-0348122:
Zhonghai Bai and a large team combined two views of a moving hand to recognise gestures from video more reliably. One view captures the hand's shape through statistical descriptors treated with special geometry that respects their curved mathematical home. The other tracks motion, summarising how brightness flows across a grid from frame to frame. Either view alone misses part of the story.

Fused together, the combined description beat both single views on two public benchmark sets, scoring above ninety-nine percent on one and above ninety-seven on the other. The representation stays compact and its parts remain interpretable, which helps developers debug mistakes. The authors aim the framework at touchless controls, sign language tools, and other systems where a camera has to read hands in real time.
plos-pone-0348522:
Daniel Merenstein and co-workers lay out a large trial plan to settle how acute sinus infections should be treated. Sinus trouble sends millions to clinics yearly and drives a fifth of antibiotic prescriptions, yet most cases are viral. Their 2026 protocol describes a practical trial in primary and urgent care across six United States regions, recruiting several thousand adults.

Patients who have not improved after nine days are assigned by chance to antibiotics, a steroid nose spray, both, or dummy pills, with salt-water rinsing kits for all. Symptom scores days later form the main measure. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. Its size should finally show which patients gain from antibiotics and which can skip them.
plos-pone-0348622:
CORRECTION: Satsuki Fukushima and co-authors correct their rat study of cell therapy for a weak heart. The study weighed ways to place muscle cells into hearts hurt by a heart attack. The note fixes a group size in the methods. It also fixes a death rate in the results and a note in a key table. A fresh, correct table comes with it.

The team also clears up a shared image. One chart panel matches a chart in linked work. The control tissue came from a joint run of two projects, a step meant to spare rats. The note adds more detail on how the rats were watched and put down.
plos-pone-0348022:
Tharwat A. Selim and colleagues surveyed the flies of Egypt's Sharkia Governorate across the seasons of 2022 and 2023, cataloguing species that carry disease and checking which bacteria ride on the common house fly. Twelve species from five families were identified. The 2026 study combined trapping counts with diversity statistics and laboratory culture of microbes from fly bodies.

The house fly dominated all year, and overall diversity dipped slightly in winter, when several blow fly species vanished. Some species held steady while others swung sharply with temperature. Four of five bacterial isolates from house fly surfaces were species capable of causing illness. The authors warn that these insects are active mechanical carriers of pathogens in the region.
plos-pone-0342122:
TongZhu Yu and colleagues improved the route-planning brain of tracked transport robots that haul materials through coal mine tunnels. These roadways are rough, narrow, and cluttered, so a robot must plan an efficient overall route yet dodge obstacles in real time. Their 2026 algorithm upgrades the classic A-star search with a two-way adaptive strategy and builds terrain risk into the cost of each path, then hands local steering to a reactive avoidance method.

In simulated mine roadways the planner steered around obstacles cleanly while producing shorter routes and finding them faster than the standard approach. Risk weighting kept paths out of dangerous ground. The authors offer the method for intelligent underground transport in mining.
plos-pone-0347122:
Erik E. Osnas re-estimated the numbers of Steller's eiders, a threatened sea duck breeding on Alaska's Arctic Coastal Plain, using flexible statistical models instead of traditional survey arithmetic. Rare and patchy birds make crude counts jumpy. His models combined survey datasets, accounted for missed birds, and mapped density across the region year by year.

The population, it turns out, breathes on a roughly six-and-a-half-year cycle, swinging between a few hundred and more than two thousand birds. Long-term growth hovers near zero. Birds concentrate in the northern survey triangle and may be shifting further north. Osnas warns that trends should compare the same phase of the cycle, or the rhythm will masquerade as decline or recovery.
plos-pone-0347422:
Stuart Flint and colleagues study how views of aging link to character traits. Their survey paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It covered more than two thousand adults aged sixty-five and up. Half lived in Britain and half in Canada. Each filled a short form on aging attitudes. Each also wrote open answers about growing older.

An AI tool read the language of those written answers. It grouped people into two character clusters. Each cluster held its own outlook on later life. The written themes tied outlooks to habits such as staying active. How people feel about aging shapes health and daily choices. Programs for older adults, the authors argue, should fit each outlook.
plos-pone-0345922:
Alexandra Ferguson and colleagues use control theory to steer a living neuron with electric current, in this 2026 PLOS ONE neuroscience paper. Their test bed is a pressure-sensing cell in the medicinal leech, and the goal is to make it fire a target signal while spending as little stimulation energy as possible.

Optimal pulses were computed in advance from a simplified model that was deliberately not fitted to the real cell. Remarkably, the living neurons lost tracking accuracy at exactly the same points as the simulated ones as energy was cut. The match suggests the model's dynamics capture something real about the cell, a step toward gentler neural stimulation for medicine.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Mines in the Corfu Channel sent Britain and Albania to the World Court in 1947. On 9 April, the Council adopted Resolution 22. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Poland and the Soviet Union held back. Britain, a party to the case, took no part. In October 1946, two British warships had struck mines in the strait. Sailors died and others were hurt.

Both governments had laid their claims before the Council. The text urges them to take the dispute to the World Court at once. The Court's statute sets the path for the case. The referral bore fruit two years later. The Corfu Channel judgment of 1949 was the Court's first full case. It still anchors the law on straits and state duty.

The world criminal court opened its doors on 1 July 2002. Days later, the Council weighed a clash. Some states with troops on UN duty were not court members. Their soldiers could, in theory, face charges at The Hague. The United States pressed hard for a shield. Resolution 1422 passed with no dissent on 12 July 2002.

The text asks the court to pause for one year. No probes or cases could start in that time. The shield guards peace staff from states outside the court. It rests on a clause in the court's own treaty, meant for just such clashes. The Council said it would renew the plea each July as long as needed. The deal kept US-backed missions alive, but it split world opinion.

Kashmir's fate came back to the table in 1957. India and Pakistan each spoke their claim. The old UN line was a free vote by the Kashmiri people. A local body in the state had called a meet to fix its path. That move rang alarms in New York. Resolution 122 passed on 24 January 1957 by ten votes to none. The Soviet team held back.

The Council stood by the vote plan. A free, fair poll, run by the UN, was still the sole lawful path. No act by the local meet could stand in for that poll. What the meet had done, or might do, could not fix the state's fate. Backing for such acts was ruled out too. The case would stay on the Council's books. The words are firm, but the poll they pledged has yet to be held.

Resolution 522 passed by a full vote on 4 October 1982. It repeats the Council's calls in the Iran-Iraq war, still with no reply. Members deplored the war's growth and its toll in lives and wrecked towns. They recalled a July text that had told both sides to cease fire and pull back. A note from the Council's chair had backed that call days later.

The Council urged an end to the war at once, in the strongest words it had used so far. Both sides were to pull back to the lines the world accepts as their borders. One side had said it would heed the July text. The Council pressed the other to match that pledge. The UN watch team for the truce had to be sent with no more delay.

Cyprus and its peacekeeping force return in Resolution 422, adopted on 15 December 1977. The Secretary-General reported that the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus was still vital to keep the island quiet and help the search for a settlement. The force's movement in the north was still limited. A high-level meeting that April had produced an agreement the Council wanted both sides to honor.

The Council extends the force's stay for six months, ending 15 June 1978, hoping that progress by then might let it shrink or withdraw. It urges the sides to show the greatest restraint and speed up joint work toward a just and peaceful solution. It asks the Secretary-General to keep his good offices mission going and to report by 31 May 1978. The text reaffirms the 1964 decision that created the force and the call for a settlement endorsed in 1974.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war draws its first Council resolution in Resolution 822, adopted on 30 April 1993. Relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan had worsened sharply, and local Armenian forces had invaded Azerbaijan's Kelbadjar district. Large numbers of civilians were displaced, creating a humanitarian emergency. A peace process was under way in the CSCE's Minsk Group, and the fighting threatened to wreck it.

The Council demands an immediate end to all hostilities and hostile acts to establish a durable ceasefire. It demands the withdrawal of all occupying forces from Kelbadjar and other recently occupied areas of Azerbaijan. It urges the parties to resume negotiations at once within the Minsk Group process. It urges them to avoid anything that blocks a peaceful settlement. It calls for unimpeded access for international relief work. The Secretary-General is asked to assess the situation in the region. He is also asked to report back.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2022 (XX), adopted on 5 November 1965, sharpened the Assembly's stand on Southern Rhodesia days before the minority regime's expected move to independence. The Assembly restated the people's right to freedom and backed their struggle. It condemned racial discrimination in the territory in the strongest terms.

The text solemnly warned that the United Nations would oppose any move to independence that was not based on a vote for every adult. It demanded freedom for political prisoners, and repeal of harsh and unfair laws such as the Land Apportionment Act. It demanded suspension of the 1961 constitution and a conference of all parties. It called on Britain to use all the means it needed, force included.

General Assembly Resolution 22, adopted on 13 February 1946, approved the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations and offered it to each member for joining. The Charter had promised the Organization the legal standing and protections it needs to do its work, and the convention spells out what those are.

The text gives the United Nations legal personality. It shields its buildings, funds, and records from search or seizure. It frees it from direct taxes and customs duties on official goods. It also grants protections to member representatives, officials, and experts on mission. It covers United Nations travel papers. It sets ways to settle disputes.

With resolution 66/222, the General Assembly declares 2014 the International Year of Family Farming. The decision rests on the view that family and smallholder farming underpin sustainable food production and food security. This holds especially for the many small farmers who are women. The Food and Agriculture Organization is invited to lead implementation. It would work with governments and other United Nations bodies. Costs beyond its existing mandate are met from voluntary contributions. Member states are encouraged to back the year through their own development programs.

Resolution 69/22 of the General Assembly keeps the special information programme going on the question of Palestine run by the Department of Public Information for 2015–2016. The programme publicizes United Nations work on Palestine. It makes and updates publications and audiovisual material. It holds fact-finding missions and seminars for journalists in the region. It trains Palestinian broadcasters and journalists each year. The Assembly treats wide, accurate public information as part of building support for a just and lasting settlement.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Violence in Jerusalem and the occupied territories, the opening bloodshed of the Second Intifada, fills this text of 7 October 2000. Clashes had followed a provocation at Al-Haram Al-Sharif on 28 September. More than 80 Palestinians were killed in the days that followed.

The Council deplored the provocation and the violence at holy places and across the territories. It condemned the excessive use of force against Palestinians and reminded Israel of its duties under the Fourth Geneva Convention. It called for the violence to stop, for a swift and fair inquiry, and for a quick return to peace talks.

Army reform in Congo wins support on 15 January 2004. The Pretoria transition deal had created a Government of National Unity and Transition. Merging the former warring forces into one national army and police was, in the Council's view, a key test of the whole transition.

Work on the first integrated, unified brigade at Kisangani is welcomed. The old demand to demilitarize Kisangani no longer applies to the restructured, integrated Congolese forces there. The government is urged to complete the merger, including setting up a Supreme Defence Council, and to press ahead with disarming and reintegrating former fighters.

Border demarcation between Ethiopia and Eritrea remained blocked when their mission, UNMEE, was extended on 13 September 2005, until 15 March 2006. Lasting peace, the Council said, was impossible without it. Concern was growing at restrictions placed on the mission and at the risk of renewed tension.

Both parties are called on to avoid any step that could lead to fighting. Ethiopia is called on to accept the Boundary Commission's ruling fully and without conditions, as the Algiers Agreements require. Both sides are also told to carry out the agreements completely and without delay. Eritrea is urged to take immediate steps, in consultation with UNMEE, to lift the limits on the mission's work and movement.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union stabilization force is renewed on 21 November 2006 for another planned twelve months. The pattern matches the renewals of 2004 and 2005: support is restated for the High Representative and for completing the 1995 peace agreement, and the status-of-forces arrangements covering the force are noted.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to keep the force under unified command. They may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace agreement's military terms, defend the force, and help it accomplish its mission. The parties are again told to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement throughout the country.

The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions regime is updated on 30 June 2008. The asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on everyone on the sanctions committee's Consolidated List are restated. The listed groups are condemned for continuing terrorist attacks on civilians and for undermining stability in Afghanistan and beyond.

Fair-process steps built up over years of criticism of the list are added. States proposing names must give as much identifying detail as possible, and the committee must publish a summary of why each name is listed. All listed names were to be reviewed by 2010 to check they still belong. Humanitarian exemptions to the asset freeze are confirmed, and the monitoring team is renewed to help the committee.

Chad and the Central African Republic host the United Nations mission called MINURCAT, and its future was under review in May 2010. A new report had just offered ideas for a changed mandate. Resolution 1922, adopted on 12 May 2010, gave the Council time to study those ideas. It extended the mission's mandate only until 26 May 2010, on the terms set in earlier resolutions. The Council said the situation in the region was still a threat to international peace and security, and it kept the matter under active review.

A transitional government had taken office in Libya on 22 November 2011, days after the war ended. Resolution 2022, adopted on 2 December 2011, concerns the United Nations Support Mission in Libya, called UNSMIL. The mission had been created for three months. Its job was to help the country in the first phase after the conflict.

The Council extended UNSMIL's mandate until 16 March 2012. It asked for a report on the next phase of United Nations support. The mission also gained an extra task. It had to help Libya's authorities deal with loose weapons left over from the war. Portable surface-to-air missiles were a special concern. Such weapons would be a danger far beyond Libya if they reached armed groups.

Portugal's African colonies came before the Council again on 22 November 1972. The territories were Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde, and Mozambique. The Organization of African Unity had recognized the liberation movements there. It treated them as the true voice of their peoples. Resolution 322 was adopted unanimously.

The Council restated the right of the peoples of those territories to govern themselves and be free. Their struggle was backed as just. Portugal was called on to stop its military operations and all repression at once. It was also told to open talks with the parties concerned. The talks would aim to end the armed conflict and reach a settlement. Portugal had to report to the Council on progress at regular intervals.
un-sc-res-22:
Two British warships struck mines in the Corfu Channel in October 1946. The blasts killed sailors and hurt others. Britain blamed Albania, and Albania denied the charge. On 9 April 1947 the Security Council heard both governments. It then pointed them toward a court instead of a quarrel.

The Council recommends that Britain and Albania refer the dispute at once to the International Court of Justice. The case became the young court's first contentious judgment. In 1949 the court held Albania responsible for the minefield. The short text thus marks an early turn to law over force.
un-sc-res-1422:
The International Criminal Court opened its doors on 1 July 2002. Eleven days later the Security Council acted to shield some peacekeepers from it. On 12 July 2002 it asked the court to hold off on certain cases. Cases over United Nations work by staff from states outside the Rome Statute were covered. The court should not start or proceed with such a case for twelve months. Article 16 of the statute allows that request.

The Council said it intended to renew the request each July. The renewal would run as long as needed. States had to avoid acts that clashed with the pause. The deal ended a standoff that had threatened peacekeeping mandates. Critics saw it as a carve-out for powerful states.
un-sc-res-122:
Kashmir's own assembly could not settle the state's future, the Council ruled in 1957. India and Pakistan had restated their cases that January. On 24 January 1957 the Council recalled the old United Nations plan for the state. The final shape of Jammu and Kashmir would come from a free vote of its people. That principle came from resolutions passed in 1948 and 1949. A commission for the two countries had framed the terms.

A constituent assembly chosen in the state could not replace that vote. Any act by such a body to fix the state's status would have no standing. The Council said it would keep considering the dispute. The Soviet Union abstained. The plebiscite at the heart of the text was never held.
un-sc-res-522:
Iran and Iraq were told again to stop the war on 4 October 1982. The Council deplored the conflict's lengthening and escalation, with heavy loss of life and damage. It recalled resolution 514 (1982), adopted that July, and the Secretary-General's report of 15 July. One party had already said it would cooperate in carrying out resolution 514. The other had not.

The Council urgently called once more for an immediate cease-fire and an end to all military operations. Its call for a withdrawal of forces to the internationally recognized boundaries was reaffirmed. The Council restated its decision to send United Nations observers to verify any cease-fire and withdrawal. Mediation efforts had to continue. All other states were asked to abstain from any act that could feed the fighting. The Secretary-General had to report on the text's working within seventy-two hours, a sign of how fast the Council wanted movement.
un-sc-res-422:
Voting on 15 December 1977, the Council adopted Resolution 422 on Cyprus. The island had been split since the fighting of 1974. A United Nations peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, set up in 1964, patrolled between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot sides.

The text extends the posting of that force in Cyprus until 15 June 1978. The Secretary-General had reported that the force stayed vital for calm and for peace talks. The Council urges both sides to show restraint and avoid acts that could raise tensions. It asks the Secretary-General to report on progress by 31 May 1978.
un-sc-res-822:
The Security Council adopted Resolution 822 on Nagorno-Karabakh on 30 April 1993. Local Armenian forces had just seized the Kelbadjar district of Azerbaijan. The attack drove large numbers of civilians from their homes. Ties between Armenia and Azerbaijan sank to a new low.

The Council demands an instant end to all fighting and hostile acts. It orders all occupying forces out of Kelbadjar and other newly taken areas of Azerbaijan. It urges both sides to return to talks in the Minsk Group peace process. Relief groups must get open access to every area hit by the conflict, the text adds.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Cyprus and its United Nations peacekeeping force are the subject of Security Council resolution 222, adopted unanimously on June 16, 1966. The force, UNFICYP, had been sent to the island in 1964 to stop fighting between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities. Its mandate ran in short spans and needed regular renewal by the Council.

Citing a report of the Secretary-General, the resolution finds that the force is still needed to keep peace on the island. It notes that Cyprus has agreed to the force staying past June 26, 1966. The text reaffirms the Council's earlier Cyprus resolutions and extends the force's stay.
europmc-pmc10763622:
Fischer led a phase 2a trial in 2022 of molnupiravir, an oral drug for early Covid-19. No easy oral drug yet blocked the virus from spreading or worsening. The trial enrolled 202 unvaccinated adults with proven infection and under seven days of symptoms. Doses of 200, 400, or 800 mg ran twice a day for five days.

The top dose cleared viral RNA a day faster than the dummy pill. Fischer reports a median of 14 days versus 15 days. By day 3, live virus showed in swabs from just 1.9% on the top dose, versus 16.7% on the dummy. By day 5, no live virus grew from the two higher dose arms. The drug was well tolerated at each dose.
europmc-pmc1174822:
Carroll revisits a 30-year-old thesis about how animal form evolves in this 2005 essay. King and Wilson proposed in 1975 that humans and chimps differ mainly in how genes are regulated, not in the proteins themselves. Their proteins were strikingly similar, too similar to explain the anatomical and behavioural gaps. Changes in the switches controlling gene expression, they argued, drive changes in anatomy and way of life.

Carroll assesses the thesis as comparative genomics and developmental biology pour forth new data, with the full chimp genome in hand. He distinguishes anatomy from physiology: coding changes clearly drive some physiological differences, such as vision and respiration. For form, though, theoretical and empirical evidence points to regulatory sequence changes as the major contributor, he argues. That conclusion challenges genomics, since regulatory DNA is hard to read.
europmc-pmc1241922:
Mahaffey, Clickner, and Bodurow analyzed blood mercury and fish intake in 2004. Data covered 1,709 women in a national survey from 1999 and 2000. The middle blood mercury value was 0.6 micrograms per liter. Values ranged from undetectable to 6.7 at the high end.

Blood mercury tracked fish and shellfish eating closely. Women aged 30 to 49 ran about 1.5 times the levels of younger women. Levels were lowest among Mexican Americans. Women who ate fish often had seven times the mercury of non-eaters. Mahaffey ties intake records to body burden with numbers. Levels ran highest in the other group, which included Asian and Pacific Islander women.
europmc-pmc1420322:
Burnham reviewed the Scopus database in 2006, a search tool for science, health, and tech journals. Scopus lets users search both older and newer work through the reference lists in each article. Libraries can use it for research and for choosing which journals to buy.

Burnham compares Scopus with its main rival, Web of Science. Neither tool covers all journals, and each fills gaps in the other. The review notes Scopus was built by Elsevier over two years, with input from 21 research sites. Burnham advises that a library which can afford just one should pick based on its own users' needs.
europmc-pmc1431722:
Malaria parasites ship proteins into the red blood cells they invade. Sargeant and co-authors hunted for those exported proteins in 2006, using new software to scan parasite genomes. They compared parasites that infect rodents with those that infect humans.

Some exported proteins were shared across both groups. Many others had grown in number in just one branch of the family. Sargeant calls this a lineage-specific expansion, growth limited to one line of descent. The pattern suggests each parasite line tailored its exported set to its own host. Such tailoring may help explain how the parasites dodge host defenses and cause disease.
europmc-pmc1513222:
Strong pain drugs carry a risk of misuse by the patients they help. Ives and co-authors followed 196 chronic pain patients on opioids for a year in 2006. Misuse meant acts like using unprescribed drugs, forging scripts, or selling pills. Urine tests helped detect it.

Sixty-two patients, 32 percent, misused opioids within the year. The most common sign was cocaine or stimulants in urine, in 40 percent of misusers. Past cocaine abuse raised the odds over four-fold. A past drug or DUI conviction and past alcohol abuse each raised odds about 2.6-fold. Younger age also tracked with misuse. Ives argues these markers can guide closer watch.
europmc-pmc1657022:
New neurons in the adult hippocampus grow dendrites, their input branches, on no fixed schedule. Plümpe and co-authors quantified that in 2006, following cells marked by the protein doublecortin. Most regulation of adult neurogenesis acts during this phase.

One fifth of marked cells were still dividing; over 70 percent were postmitotic, done dividing. The trip to full dendrite maturity took from three days to several weeks. Pushing precursor division up or down did not change dendrite timing. Plümpe concludes maturation starts at varying times after division ends, governed by its own micro-regulation.
europmc-pmc1968522: Cellular accumulation of the anticancer agent cisplatin: a review. — a 2005 science paper on cisplatin buildup. It checks the cell buildup for labs. The paper is the buildup review: the notes on cancer drugs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2002422: Breast cancer and atypia among young and middle-aged women: a study of 110 medicolegal autopsies. — a 2005 science paper on breast atypia autopsies. It studies the 110 autopsies. The paper is the autopsy study: the findings on breast ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2276522: Cytological and transcript analyses reveal fat and lazy persister-like bacilli in tuberculous sputum. — a 2005 science paper on sleepy TB germs. It reveals the persister bacilli. The paper is the persister study: the findings on TB, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2323222: Transcriptional recapitulation and subversion of embryonic colon development by mouse colon tum — a 2008 science paper on colon tumors re-running development. It finds the recapitulation. The paper is the recapitulation study: the findings on colon ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2409622: Detection of curcumin and its metabolites in hepatic tissue and portal blood of patients follow — a 2008 science paper on curcumin in liver and blood. It detects the curcumin metabolites. The paper is the detection study: the findings on curcumin, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2535622: Public Health and Air Pollution in Asia (PAPA): a multicity study of short-term effects of air — a 2008 science paper on the PAPA study. It studies the multicity effects. The paper is the PAPA study: the findings on pollution, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2637922: Active-site inhibitors of mTOR target rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 and mTORC2. — a 2008 science paper on mTOR inhibitors. It targets the rapamycin-resistant outputs. The paper is the inhibitor study: the findings on mTOR ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2732522: Worldwide occurrence of Beijing/W strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis: a systematic review. — a 2008 science paper on Beijing/W TB strains. It reviews the systematic occurrence. The paper is the strain review: the findings on Beijing ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2736622: Chronic cyclodextrin treatment of murine Niemann-Pick C disease ameliorates neuronal cholestero — a 2008 science paper on cyclodextrin treatment. It ameliorates the murine disease. The paper is the treatment study: the findings on Niemann-Pick ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2765422: Consanguinity and reproductive health among Arabs. — a 2008 science paper on consanguinity. It studies the reproductive health. The paper is the consanguinity study: the findings on Arab ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily still.
ptolemy-tetrabiblos-ashmand-1822:
Claudius Ptolemy, Alexandria's great astronomer, also wrote the Tetrabiblos on astrology. J. M. Ashmand's English translation appeared in 1822 with notes and appendices. The work became the most important surviving ancient text on its subject.

Ptolemy sets out how planets were believed to shape weather and nations. Individual lives, births, and fortunes receive systematic treatment in later books. Appendices add extracts from his Almagest and the Centiloquy attributed to him. Believer or skeptic, readers cannot understand two thousand years of star lore without it. Ashmand's version served English astrologers and historians throughout the nineteenth century. It set the terms for all who came after it in the field.
lancre-incredulite-sortilege-french-1622:
Pierre de Lancre, the Bordeaux judge who had presided over the Labourd witch trials, published his second great treatise in 1622. Its title announces its target: the incredulity and unbelief of the age about sorcery. De Lancre refutes the doubters with apparitions, pacts, and sabbaths set out at length.

The book is his demonological summa, the full-dress statement of his creed. He writes as a judge who saw the evidence and burned the condemned. Skeptics, in his view, shield the devil's servants. Few works defend the persecution with such learning and such confidence. De Lancre's summa shows the witch-judge answering his critics from the height of his own certainty.
plos-pone-0004922:
Gene-chip studies scan thousands of genes at once. They hunt for molecular signatures of disease. But a signature found by luck helps no one. Constantin Aliferis and co-authors examined this problem in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked what gives complex microarray analysis enough statistical power. Powered studies produce signatures that hold up.

The team tested how design choices change reliability. Sample size and analysis method both mattered. So did the checks used to confirm significance. Their work maps the trade-offs researchers face when planning a study. It offers practical guidance for building gene-based tests that other labs can reproduce.
plos-pone-0005022:
Type A influenza infects many animals. Its hosts include humans, pigs, horses, marine mammals and birds. Shuo Liu and colleagues mapped the whole family's diversity. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The viruses sort into sixteen hemagglutinin subtypes. They also sort into nine neuraminidase subtypes. Combinations of these define the strains.

The study charted the phylogeny and distribution of all these viruses. It shows how flu diversity spreads across hosts and regions. The panorama is a baseline for surveillance. Tracking the next pandemic strain starts from such maps. The work also reveals how freely flu genes move between species. That movement is what makes this virus so hard to corner.
plos-pone-0005122:
Gene therapy needs viruses that home to the right tissues. Peptide libraries displayed on viral capsids can select such homing. Stefan Michelfelder and colleagues tried the selection inside living animals. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The virus was adeno-associated virus. Random peptide libraries decorated its surface. Biopanning in vivo did the selecting.

The screen successfully expanded the virus's tropism. It did not achieve complete restriction to one tissue. The virus reached new targets but kept old ones too. The study maps both promise and limits of steering viruses. Future work must add restriction to expansion. Knowing the gap is progress. It tells engineers what problem to solve next.
plos-pone-0005222:
A popular lab recipe claims that chemicals can turn rat bone marrow stem cells into neuron-like cells. Many labs have used that recipe and reported success. Barnabé and colleagues put the claim to a stricter test in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Treated mesenchymal stem cells did take on molecular traits of neurons, as the title states. But they lacked the basic functional properties that real neurons must have, such as proper electrical behavior. The gap between looking like a neuron and acting like one is a warning for stem cell claims.
plos-pone-0005322:
Reproduction in mammals is governed by neurons that release GnRH, a hormone that starts the whole fertility chain. Those neurons take in signals about time of day and energy balance. Ward and colleagues mapped the peptidergic neurons that wire into GnRH neurons in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Peptide-releasing neurons conveying circadian and energy information connect directly to the GnRH cells. That wiring explains how clocks and hunger can gate fertility. The map is basic anatomy with broad reach, from farm breeding to human fertility disorders. Hunger and the clock both speak to the cells that start puberty and keep adult health on track. And this wiring map shows the lines those talks travel on, day and night, in the mouse brain.
plos-pone-0005922:
Young brain cells must know when to stop dividing and start their real work. In 2009, Shigeru Tanaka, Imran Shaikh, Antonio Chiocca and colleagues studied that switch in the cerebellum of young rodents. Their PLOS ONE paper centers on GPR3, a receptor linked to the Gs protein, in granule cell precursors.

The title states the core result: GPR3 holds back the growth of these young cells as they move and mature after birth. Without such a brake, the cerebellum could not build its layers on schedule. The work names one of the stop signals that shape the growing brain and may guide later studies of brain growth gone wrong.
plos-pone-0006022:
Citation counts have long been the coin of scientific worth, yet science now lives online. Johan Bollen, Herbert Van de Sompel, Aric Hagberg and colleagues gathered thirty-nine rival measures of impact in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper runs a principal component analysis, a method that finds the few big patterns hiding in many measures at once.

If most measures collapse into a few shared dimensions, then impact is simpler than the crowd of metrics suggests. The study helps universities and funders judge work with their eyes open. It also marks a moment when the field began, in earnest, to grade itself with more than the citation count alone.
plos-pone-0006122:
A trusted lab drug turned out to carry a stowaway. Carlos Lafourcade, Longhua Zhang and Bradley Alger report in 2009 that a contaminant of DHPG, a standard agonist for group I metabotropic glutamate receptors, suppresses GABA release on its own. Their PLOS ONE paper shows the suppression runs through neither the mGluR nor the CB1 receptor routes it was credited to.

Group I receptors, types 1 and 5, are central to neuronal communication, so work built on DHPG is widespread. A contaminant doing the real work puts past results at risk of misreading. The paper is a standing warning on reagent purity, and it gives labs a reason to check a shelf staple before building on it.
plos-pone-0006222:
An enzyme called prolyl oligopeptidase, or POP, has been linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Gemma Comellas and colleagues designed test substrates for it in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used the one-bead one-compound method, where each tiny bead carries a different candidate molecule.

The study reports the first solid-phase substrates made for POP. Good substrates let scientists measure the enzyme's activity quickly and screen blockers against it. Those screens are early steps toward drugs for brain disorders tied to POP. The bead method itself shows how to build test molecules for other enzymes.
plos-pone-0006722:
Tamaki Wada and colleagues reported an efficient way to make spinal motor neurons from stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Severe motor neuron diseases have no cures or strong treatments. Getting real spinal motor neurons from human tissue is extremely hard. Technical and ethical barriers both stand in the way. Embryonic stem cells offer an alternative source.

The method works with human and monkey embryonic stem cells. It differentiates them into spinal motor neurons with high efficiency. It also enriches the neurons so cultures are purer. Reliable supplies of these neurons support disease research in the dish. They also support testing of possible drugs before animal or human trials.
plos-pone-0006822:
Peter Lapan, Jing Zhang, and Andrew Hill used imaging to watch cancer cells change through direct contact in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell-to-cell contact controls many key processes. Metastatic tumor cells colonize new sites through such interactions. Stem cells also take cues from their niche neighbors. Laboratory methods often miss contact effects by growing cells apart.

Their image-based assessment captured growth and signaling changes in contacting cells. Pictures over time reveal behavior that single snapshots hide. Contact-driven changes could explain steps in metastasis. They could also guide how stem cells are cultured. The method gives cell biologists a window on interaction itself.
plos-pone-0006922:
Li Zhou, Yoshiharu Takayama, Philippe Boucher, and colleagues reported a cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined a protein called LRP1 in the walls of blood vessels. LRP1 helps guard against atherosclerosis, the clogging of arteries. It does so by controlling a growth signal receptor in vascular smooth muscle cells.

The team traced how LRP1 limits activation of that receptor, known as PDGFRβ. They followed the signal into a downstream pathway involving phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase. Their results explain how vessel wall structure stays orderly. The findings matter for understanding how arteries harden and narrow in disease.
plos-pone-0007022:
Ole Søgaard, Nicolai Lohse, Jan Gerstoft, and colleagues studied pneumonia outcomes in HIV in PLOS ONE in 2009. People with HIV face a raised risk of pneumonia. That risk persists even on modern antiretroviral treatment. The team used a nationwide Danish cohort covering 1995 to 2008.

They measured death rates after a hospital stay for pneumonia. They also searched for factors that predicted who would die. Such prognostic knowledge guides care for a still-vulnerable group. It shows where extra monitoring or earlier treatment might save lives in the treatment era. The nationwide cohort gives those patterns a population-wide base.
plos-pone-0007122:
Marta Bull, Gerald Learn, Indira Genowati, and colleagues examined HIV in the female genital tract in PLOS ONE in 2009. Earlier studies suggested the virus there forms compartments separate from blood. Those studies covered fifty-seven women in total and mostly used free virus. The team looked again, comparing cell-free and cell-associated virus in women with chronic infection.

They found the genital tract virus was not a distinct population. It consisted of uniform, low-diversity variants instead. That distinction matters for transmission and prevention research. What leaves the body may be a narrow sample of the virus, not a separate strain.
plos-pone-0007222:
Nicholas J. Gibson, Leslie P. Tolbert, and Lynne A. Oland studied the developing sense of smell in PLOS ONE in 2009. Olfactory receptor neurons send axons into the brain. With help from glial cells, those axons sort into bundles aimed at specific glomeruli, the smell-processing units.

The authors examine special membrane lipid domains in this system. They ask how those domains affect EGF receptor activation and the stability of cell adhesion molecules. Their work explains part of how a developing olfactory system wires itself into stable, working smell circuits in insects.
plos-pone-0007322:
Kentaro Q. Sakamoto, Akinori Takahashi, Takashi Iwata, and colleagues attached cameras to albatrosses in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Albatrosses fly hundreds of kilometers across open ocean to find prey. Despite growing work on their foraging behavior, little was known about how the birds actually locate food at sea.

The team used a bird-borne camera to see the ocean from the albatross's view. They report an association between albatrosses and a killer whale in the Southern Ocean. Following large predators may help the birds find prey. The footage gives rare direct evidence of that strategy.
openalex-w2023168822: How long does a puff of CO2 warm the planet? A 2013 team study computed CO2 and climate response curves for greenhouse gas metrics. The work underpinned Global Warming Potential and temperature-potential math used by policymakers.
openalex-w2037838222: Chlorophyll fluorescence answers plant questions — this FAQ tells how. Kalaji and colleagues' 2014 educational review answers frequently asked questions about in vivo chlorophyll fluorescence. The Q&A format covered hardware, methods, and hands-on application for beginners.
openalex-w2098318922: ATLAS measures electron energies to fine precision. The ATLAS collaboration's 2014 paper presents electron and photon energy calibration using LHC Run 1 data. The calibration, built on ~25 fb−1 of 7 and 8 TeV collisions, tuned the detector's energy scale.
openalex-w2106898322: Beans feed millions — drought threatens them. Beebe and colleagues' 2013 paper covers phenotyping common beans for adaptation to drought. The work guided breeding for dry highlands and coasts across the tropics and subtropics — where beans matter most for dinner.
openalex-w2109200822: Breathing strength needs reference numbers. A 1999 study set reference values for breathing pressures and ventilation. The work gave Brazilian clinicians norms for respiratory muscle strength in health and disease — the numbers behind the tests, measured right and published.
openalex-w2148047822: Lead collisions flowed — ATLAS measured the pattern. The ATLAS team's 2012 paper measured particle flow patterns in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV. The measurements probed the collision's teamwork — flow's mark, caught at last by physicists now — flow's story.
plos-pone-0006322:
When T cells switch on to fight infection, hundreds of their proteins change level. Wei-Yun Sheng and Tzu-Chien Wang profiled those changes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper using proteomics, a survey of the full protein set. Very little was known about what the differentially expressed proteins actually do in activated T cells.

The survey found the energy enzyme GAPDH inside the nucleus of activated T lymphocytes. A familiar metabolic workhorse appearing in the nucleus suggests a second job. Proteomic maps generate such surprises systematically. Following them up can reveal new layers of immune control.
plos-pone-0009722:
Transcription factors are proteins that grip DNA at set spots and switch genes on or off. Rahul Siddharthan set out to predict those grip spots more accurately. His method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding the spots by experiment alone is slow and costly.

The classic tool, the position weight matrix, scores each DNA letter on its own. The new dinucleotide version scores pairs of neighboring letters instead. Pairs carry information that single letters miss. Better scores mean better guesses at where regulators bind, which guides gene studies. The method builds directly on the classic matrix rather than replacing it.
openalex-w2488220022: Microsatellites — short, stuttering repeats of DNA — are workhorses of plant genetics, used in everything from breeding to forensics. This 2016 review explains what these single sequence repeats are, the theory behind them, and why they've stayed useful for decades across low- and high-throughput genotyping. It's a primer on one of genetics' most enduring tools.
openalex-w2614578122: Heart disease remains humanity's biggest killer, but its toll varies wildly by place. Vishal Parmar and Ignazio Bombaci study the crust of neutron stars with Bayesian methods and a unified matter model. Neutron star crust is the solid outer layer of the densest known stars. Their framework uses a relativistic mean-field description of dense matter throughout. The analysis focuses on probability distributions for crust properties. Several kinds of evidence constrain those distributions.

The constraints come from nuclear experiments, chiral effective field theory, and multi-messenger neutron star observations. Bayesian methods let all three speak at once, with uncertainty kept visible. Crust properties affect how neutron stars cool, spin down, and emit gravitational waves. A unified model avoids stitched-together descriptions of different layers. The paper speaks to nuclear astrophysicists who need crust estimates with honest error bars.
