A Cosmoglobe team builds a unified model of large-scale thermal dust emission across microwave and infrared bands. They fit a four-component dust model to COBE-DIRBE data between 3.5 and 240 micrometers. The work sits inside the global Bayesian end-to-end Cosmoglobe DR2 reanalysis. Their 2026 preprint is part seven of that series. A concordance model is the goal: one description that fits many data sets at once.

Dust emission blocks and biases views of the cosmic microwave background. A model that works from infrared to microwave frequencies helps separate dust from the primordial signal. Four components let different dust populations glow in their own ways. Bayesian end-to-end analysis keeps instrument effects inside the same fit. The paper speaks to cosmologists who clean microwave maps. It also serves scholars who study galactic dust itself.
arxiv-2601-07922:
Krystian Iłkiewicz and colleagues report a bow shock around a white dwarf that has no accretion disk. Bow shocks form when an outflow meets the interstellar medium. In white dwarfs that accrete from a companion, outflows usually come from a donor wind, the disk, or a surface explosion. A diskless accreting white dwarf should not obviously drive one. Yet the team finds a persistent bow shock around such a system. Their 2026 preprint presents the case.

Persistence matters: a steady shock needs a steady outflow to sustain it. Finding one without a disk challenges the usual list of outflow sources. Magnetism may play a role, as the system is a magnetised accretor. The result pushes astronomers to rethink how these binaries shed matter and energy. The paper serves scholars on cataclysmic variables and white dwarf binaries. It is an observational puzzle with theoretical consequences.
arxiv-2601-07022:
The Upstage Solar Team posted a 2026 arXiv report on a new large language model called Solar Open. Solar Open has 102 billion settings, called parameters. It works in two languages. It is built as a Mixture-of-Experts model, where each chunk of text is sent to a few expert parts, not the whole model. The report aims at languages that most models serve poorly.

The team lays out a clear method for how such a model can match strong rivals. They name three linked tasks that drive the work. The first task is data. Scant data in the target languages makes training hard. To fix that, the team made 4.5 trillion tokens of new data. The data is of high grade, tied to set fields, and shaped for later reward-based training. The report tells builders how the whole build was done.
arxiv-2601-08522: Louis Gaillard wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on bounds for the degree of solutions to two kinds of equations. The kinds are linear differential equations and recurrences. Such equations show much about their own solutions. They also serve as neat forms to store solutions, for sums with special functions. Gaillard finds a large class of methods that build such forms. Each method builds a linear link between steps of a basic operator called a pseudo-linear map. The bounds cap the size of what those methods produce.
arxiv-2601-08822:
D. Pauli and eight co-authors study the most huge stars and how they shed mass. Huge stars pour out light and wind. That flow shapes the space round them and once helped clear the early fog of the cosmos. Yet the life path of such stars is still not well known, so their true flow is hard to gauge.

The team looks at mass loss when a star nears its light cap. Past that cap, light push can throw off whole shells of gas at once. Such bursts can change the star mass fast and shift its whole late life. A reader in star work gets a fresh take on those bursts. They may be a main key to how huge stars end.
arxiv-2601-09522:
Badr-Eddine Marani and five co-authors work on making neural network predictions honest about doubt. Their 2026 arXiv paper adapts conformal prediction to each class separately. Deep networks often sound sure even when they are wrong, and their stated probabilities can mislead.

Conformal prediction wraps a model's output in a set with a guaranteed coverage rate. A single global rule, though, can give some classes loose sets and others tight ones. Class-adaptive training aims to even that out while learning. Fairer uncertainty matters most where a wrong, confident answer is costly, as in medical imaging.
arxiv-2601-10022:
Dilipkumar Asthagiri and Dmitry Matyushov track how water holds a twist over time. In a fluid, a twist does not fade at a flat rate. Past twists shape how the next twist fades. This drag from the past is named a memory effect. It bends the fade curve from a plain exp form.

Such memory curves had not been worked out for the spin of water. The pair now do that math. They treat one water unit on its own. They also treat the full sample as one whole. The test case is the SPC/E model of water. The curves aid work on how fluids move and react.
arxiv-2601-10122:
Ye Wang, Jiaxing Chen, and Hongjiang Xiao map the state of role play agents. These agents act as a set role in talk. They may play a guide, a peer, or a famed name. Large language models gave this field a fresh push.

The paper sorts past work in three waves. First came rule based forms with set lines. Next came style copy, where agents learned how a role talks. Last came mind copy, with traits and memory at the core. The team lists what each wave can do. They also name what still blocks the field and where it may go next.
arxiv-2601-10522:
Federico Malizia, Andrés Guzmán, Federico Battiston, and István Kiss study how nested sets speed or curb spread on a hypergraph. In such a net, a set can hold an other set in full. That nest form is named nested hyperedges. Spread here can be a germ, a tale, or a trend.

The team build a theory for spread on such nets. Nested sets help spread start at a lower point. Yet they curb the sharp jump form of spread. That jump is named explosive behavior. The twin acts were not both known till now. The work ties micro form to macro acts.
arxiv-2601-10722:
Daniel Casini, Jian-Jia Chen, Jing Li, Federico Reghenzani, and Harun Teper survey real-time support in ROS 2. ROS 2 is the middleware that ties robot software parts together. It offers modular design, spread-out execution, and rich communication. Robots that must react on a strict clock need more than that: they need timing they can count on.

Over the last six years, both researchers and industry have pushed ROS 2 toward hard real-time use. The survey gathers the support, the analysis methods, and the latest advances. It maps what is proven, what is patched, and what is still missing. Teams building time-critical robots get a guide to what ROS 2 can promise today.
arxiv-2601-10622:
Yu-Han Ni, Chao Wu, and Jiang-Hao Yu build amplitudes for massive particles in the Standard Model. Amplitudes give the odds of particle processes. Working in the minimal helicity-chirality frame, they construct amplitudes with more legs from basic blocks. The blocks are contact amplitudes with three and four particles.

The four-point contact terms turn out to be needed. Without them, gauge invariance breaks in the broken Standard Model. That symmetry is what keeps the theory consistent. A recipe like this speeds up the math for events with heavy particles. It extends an earlier massless-massive correspondence the authors set out in part one.
arxiv-2601-10822:
Jeffrey Davis and co-authors present a framework for choosing the best observables at the Large Hadron Collider. An observable is a measured pattern in collision data. Some patterns are far more sensitive to new physics than others. The team integrates analytic methods with machine learning to compute observables that are optimal for effective field theory and wider uses.

They also introduce a new metric for judging how well such methods perform. Better observables mean each collision yields more evidence. At a machine where new particles may hide in rare corners, that gain matters. The work helps collider physicists squeeze the most physics from data they already collect.
arxiv-2601-11022:
Sravan Danda, Aditya Challa, Shlok Mehendale, and Snehanshu Saha adapt models at test time by matching geometric quantiles. Test-time adaptation adjusts a classifier when test data drift from training data. Most methods tweak the model's weights, tying them to one architecture. The authors seek a method that serves transformers and convolutional networks alike.

Their approach matches high-dimensional geometric quantiles between training and test data. Quantiles summarize a distribution's shape, so matching them can realign a model without deep surgery. Drift is the norm in deployed vision: new cameras, weather, and sites all shift the data. A broad, architecture-free adapter could keep models accurate where they actually run.
arxiv-2601-12022:
Amir Dalal, Vladyslav Kozii, and Jonathan Ruhman test if broken symmetry can kill a route to superconductivity. The Kohn-Luttinger route makes superconductivity from pure repulsion between electrons. Its first proof needs full rotational symmetry.

Real materials have only discrete symmetries, such as those of a crystal grid. The team ask how strong that break must be to stop the effect. If the route is robust, more plain materials could host it. Their work sets bounds on that robustness with care.  The bounds show how much break the route can stand.  If it holds, plain repulsive matter could pair in more cases than thought.
arxiv-2601-12222:
Yishan Lv, Jing Luo, Boyuan Ju, and their co-authors grade the beauty of AI-made songs. Generative AI now makes much music, so auto grades are needed. Past work deals with speech, plain audio, or singing quality, not song beauty as such.

Most tools guess one exact mean opinion score. That misses the nuance of how humans judge beauty. Their method uses multi-stem attention, which splits a song into parts, plus a model of doubt in ranks. A richer grade could guide music tools with more taste.  Doubt aware grades fit how fans judge songs too.
arxiv-2601-11222:
Haochen Wu, Heng Wu, and Benzhuo Lu teach neural nets to solve equations. Their 2026 preprint deals with linear PDEs, a core class in applied math. For some of these, a known base solution shape exists. The team builds its whole method around that fact.

Most operator learning needs data from the full domain. Their frame trains on edge data alone, by sharp contrast. It uses the values and slopes found on the boundary. Fake data from the base solution feeds the training set. Edge integral tools add the rest of the math needed. The mix aims at fast solves that still respect the boundary.
arxiv-2601-11622:
Hassan Ugail and Newton Howard read language models as systems that change in time. Their 2026 preprint seeks working regimes inside LLMs. Text writing runs through vast inner workings in the model. How those workings unfold in time is poorly understood.

Most work on reading models stresses static states instead. Causal interventions are the other common lens in the field. Both leave temporal structure largely unexplored, they argue. The team borrows concepts from neuroscience for the task. Temporal integration and metastability mark neural organization there. They adapt those ideas to transformer models here. A combined time metric is computed from activations. It is tracked across step-by-step text writing in the model.
arxiv-2601-13222:
Laura Dietz and co-authors fold judged facts into text that AI writes from sources. Their line of work joins auto judging into retrieval augmented generation, where a model writes with docs in hand. The aim is text that can be checked, fact by fact.

Their system is called Crucible. It builds a bank of question and answer bits, called nuggets, from the docs it pulls. Each nugget keeps a clear link to its source. The bank then guides how text is drawn out, picked, and put into a report. For teams that need sourced text, the route keeps claims tied to proof as the text is built, not just checked at the end.
arxiv-2601-13422:
Dahai Yu and co-authors guess home level energy use in a frame built for trust. Such guesses aid grid runs, build plans, and storm reply. Many deep tools for the task miss one of two needs. Some skip how homes sway each other in space. Some cannot scale to one guess per home.

Their frame is called TrustEnergy. It aims for both fine scale and sound doubt. A guess per home with a trust score fits how grid teams act, by block and by home. For firms, a fine guess they can trust beats a sharp guess they cannot check. The frame joins the two in one build.
arxiv-2601-13522:
Shuang Li speeds up low rank tensor sense for Tucker forms by a chance based step swap rule. Tensor sense works back a big multi way array from few reads. Low Tucker rank forms are prized since they hold multi mode plans in small room. Past tools project the full array at dear cost, or split it yet still sum full gradients.

Their rule is called StoTAM. It swaps steps in a round and uses chance picks in place of full sums. Each step then works on a part of the task, not the whole. For signal and learn teams with huge arrays, a cheaper step can be the gap of a run that ends and one that times out.
arxiv-2601-12422:
Jiri Blazek and five co authors work on cosmic ray air showers. When an ultra high energy cosmic ray hits the air, it spawns a vast cascade of particles. Models of how hadrons collide drive how that cascade grows. Three generic traits of those collisions matter a lot: cross section, elasticity, and multiplicity.

The team present a way to tweak those three traits on purpose. They then run full three dimensional simulations of the showers. Any observable can be checked to see how much each tweak moves it. This gives a clean test of how much model doubt flows into real data. Their work was prepared as a preprint for a leading physics journal.
arxiv-2601-12522:
Asif Mohammed Samir and Mohammad Masudur Rahman work on finding bugs in code with AI agents. Bugs cost tech firms billions of dollars each year. Developers spend roughly half of their time on bug resolution. One key step is localization: finding which parts of the code are at fault.

Older methods score each code part on its own, by how suspicious it looks. That view misses how parts connect across a codebase. A fault often makes sense only when links between methods and files are seen. The team give agents two aids: formed hypotheses and dynamic cognition. Their paper was set for a program comprehension venue in 2026. Better localization could cut a large share of debugging time.
arxiv-2601-12622:
N. J. C. Spooner and colleagues report direct measurements of thoron gas coming off detector materials. Thoron is radon 220, a radioactive gas that seeps from many solids. Radon is a major background in rare event physics, where tiny signals hide easily. Measuring how much gas a material emits is a key way to control that background.

Most past emanation work targeted radon 222, the dominant isotope for these backgrounds. Thoron has been measured far less, despite its own risks. The team measure thoron emanation inside the chamber itself, a direct approach. Rare event searches, like dark matter hunts, need such care at every step. A missed background can fake a discovery, so these checks matter.
arxiv-2601-12822:
Wenqi Zhang and five co authors defend computer use agents against malicious instructions. These agents use large foundation models to operate systems through graphical interfaces. They can perform complex tasks autonomously on a real machine. That autonomy introduces serious security risks, though. Malicious instructions or visual prompt injections can trigger unsafe reasoning.

Unsafe reasoning can lead to harmful system level actions before a human notices. Their system is called MirrorGuard. It works toward secure agents via simulation to real reasoning correction, per the title. Testing reasoning in simulation first could catch bad plans safely. The work serves the safe deployment of agents that click, type, and run commands.
arxiv-2601-14122: Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul study weighted zero-sum constants for sequences over a finite field in 2026. A sequence over the field of p elements is weighted zero-sum if set weights make its weighted sum vanish. The weights here come from a set tied to the p-adic valuation. Constants in this area give the smallest length that forces such a pattern.
arxiv-2601-14222:
Tiziano Schiavone and co-authors revisit matter creation as a driver of cosmic acceleration in 2026. The persistent Hubble tension motivates alternatives to standard cosmology. So does the lack of a fundamental explanation for dark energy. Gravitationally induced particle creation is a phenomenological non-equilibrium process.

It can effectively mimic a dynamical dark-energy component in the late universe. The team places observational constraints on this matter creation process. They test it against the Hubble tension, the mismatch in expansion rate measures. A viable mimic would ease two puzzles with one mechanism. The tests use real sky data, not just toy runs. A model that fits the data and eases the tension would earn a close look.
arxiv-2601-14422:
Jackson H. O'Donnell leads a team on a strong gravitational lens in this 2026 paper. The lens is a galaxy cluster known as the Carousel lens, at redshift 0.49. Its gravity bends light from galaxies behind it. The team presents a spectroscopic survey of the field. They measured both field galaxies and lensed sources near the cluster.

Spectroscopy spreads light into a spectrum, which yields redshifts and chemical clues. This paper is the first in a series, marked by the Roman numeral in its title. Readers get the survey base for the Carousel field: who is there, at what distance, and which sources the lens magnifies.
arxiv-2601-14522:
Hunjae Lee and Corey Clark analyze how transformers move information in this 2026 paper. In decoder-only, causal transformers, the computation graph is set by causal masking. Information flows through direct-path attention. It also flows through indirect paths formed by intermediate tokens. The authors name those indirect paths runways.

They argue that certain failure modes of causal transformers trace to a misalignment. The direct and indirect modes of propagation do not line up as they should. A growing body of recent work reports the failures they study. Their title calls the effect the runway cascade. Readers get a new lens for why causal models stumble in patterned ways.
arxiv-2601-14722:
Surapon Nonesung and four co-authors present a Thai document model in this 2026 paper. Document extraction is a core component of digital workflows. Existing vision-language models predominantly favor high-resource languages. Thai presents additional challenges. Its script uses non-Latin letters, and it lacks explicit word boundaries. Real-world Thai documents are also often highly unstructured.

Those traits limit the effectiveness of current open-source models. The team's model, Typhoon OCR, is an open vision-language model for Thai document extraction. The need is wide. Thai forms run from bank slips to old state files, and most tools read them poorly. Readers get a tool built for a language most OCR systems treat as an afterthought, tested on the messy documents Thai offices actually handle.
arxiv-2601-15722:
Xiuling Wang, Xin Huang, Haibo Hu, and Jianliang Xu cut communication costs in federated graph learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks learn well from graph-structured data. Federated versions train across decentralized data holders. That setup protects privacy but creates heavy traffic. Sharing graph data or updates between sites is costly. It can also leak structure that holders want to keep.

The authors use generative diffusion modeling to ease the load. The title promises communication-efficient federated graph classification. Diffusion models can synthesize stand-in data, reducing what must be sent. Classification across graphs held by banks, hospitals, or platforms is the use case. For federated learning, communication is often the true bottleneck. Cutting it widens where the method can run.
arxiv-2601-15122:
Parviz Ahmadov and Masoud Mansoury tackle a skew in recommender systems called popularity bias. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the way a few hit items hog attention. Most items stay underexposed, which hurts both quality and fairness of exposure.

Past fixes help somewhat, but they rarely show how they work. The authors move from insight to intervention. They steer single neurons inside the model in a way that can be read and checked. That steering aims to curb the bias while keeping the system's choices open and transparent to its users.
arxiv-2601-15222:
Stavrow A. Bahnam, Robin Ferede, and a Delft team teach a drone to race at champion level with one camera. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with autonomous drone racing. The sport pushes light flying robots to their physical limits.

The onboard AI must run under tight limits on weight, power, and time. Most racing systems lean on richer sensing. MonoRace takes a robust monocular approach instead. A single camera feeds the AI that steers the drone around the track. The paper reports how this lean setup reaches true champion-level racing speed.
arxiv-2601-16122:
Jörg Schröder and Maximilian Vorwerk set out a step rule for maths of small magnets. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Landau Lifshitz Gilbert maths. That maths tracks how the magnet dir shifts in time. Steps must keep the length of the magnet dir fixed. Drift in length breaks the sense of the result.

The pair use a growth based step that holds length by form. They show the step keeps the true build of the maths. It also keeps key traits like energy loss in line. A sound step lets codes run magnet acts with trust. The work serves teams who model thin magnet films and gear.
arxiv-2601-16622:
Lin Huang and coauthors build on the fly fair gaze with straight store cost. Their 2026 preprint, named E2Former-V2, deals with graph nets for 3D atom sets. Such nets must treat turns and shifts of the set as same. Past top builds make dense parts for each edge in the set. Dense parts blow up store cost as sets grow large.

On the fly gaze skips dense parts and keeps store straight. Straight store lets the net run on big atom sets. Big sets span drugs, stuff and cell parts of real worth. The work seeks scale for fair atom nets. It tests speed and grade side by side.
arxiv-2601-16722:
Martina Alutto, Qiulin Xu, Fabrizio Dabbene, Hideaki Ishii, and Chiara Ravazzi model how green habits spread. Their 2026 preprint joins two forces in one frame. One force is peer talk, which shapes what folks think. The next force is use, which grows by spread from user to user. Each force feeds back on the next.

The team then asks how to steer the spread well. A plan-ahead control picks nudges over time. The web of links has more than one layer. Such tools could help towns push clean acts. They could also warn where push plans may fail.
arxiv-2601-16822:
Andrei Antonov, Pietro Bisio, Mariangela Bondì, Andrea Celentano, Anna Marini, and Luca Marsicano build a part for a dark matter hunt. The NA64 test at CERN fires positron beams at a thick block. Dark bits, if made, would slip out unseen. The miss in energy would be the clue. Their 2026 preprint tests a gauge block named POKERINO.

The block must gauge beam energy with fine care. The team built a first model and ran beam tests. They checked its spread and drift with care. A sound gauge keeps false clues out of the hunt. It also sharpens the true miss mark if dark bits exist.
arxiv-2601-16922:
Navid Ardeshir, Samuel Deng, Daniel Hsu, and Jingwen Liu sharpen how much data group learning needs. Group learning must do well for each crowd in a pool. Crowds may overlap, and their count can be vast. Their 2026 preprint studies a case where each crowd's aim can be hit in full. In that case, less data is needed than in the loose case.

Plain risk cuts over the right class give the gain. The gain holds though crowd count is not fin. It needs just a fin gauge of crowd shape. Less data per task cuts cost in fair AI work. Such work spans loans, health, and school tools.
arxiv-2601-17222:
Jonathan Soriano and six co-authors work on redshift measures for galaxies. Redshift tells how far a galaxy is and how the cosmos has grown. Spectra give exact values, but they are slow to take. Photos give rough values fast, a method called photometric redshift. Machine learning models do much of that work today.

The catch is range. Most models train on spectra-linked sets and fit few galaxy types. The team tests ways to widen that range. They also work on honest doubt ranges for each guess. Broad, trusted redshift maps help map galaxy growth. They also sharpen tests of the cosmos as a whole.
arxiv-2601-17522:
A. Mantile and A. Posilicano study the acoustic operator with piecewise constant coefficients. The operator models sound in media split into zones. Each zone is a bounded Lipschitz domain with its own speed and density. Transmission conditions link the zones at their borders. The authors work out the resolvent and spectrum of the operator. They also study its resonances.

Resonances govern how sound rings and decays in such media. They matter for room acoustics, sonar, and medical ultrasound. A firm spectral picture guides safe simulation. It also shows where energy can trap. The work is core analysis for wave physics. Piecewise media are the rule in real materials, not the exception.
arxiv-2601-17822:
Khlood Alharthi and Paul Stevenson study ripples in the shape of atomic nuclei. Their 2026 preprint is about octupole excitations. These are states in which the nucleus wobbles in a pear-like way around its steady shape. Each wobble tests what the matter inside the nucleus is like. Shape changes probe how the matter handles squeeze, surface stretch, and shifts between proton and neutron parts.

The paper focuses on the role of surface energy in these states. The surface of a nucleus acts a bit like the skin of a drop, and its stiffness shapes the wobble. Pinning down that role helps link lab data to the physics of nuclear matter. Such links feed into models of stars and of how nuclei hold together.
arxiv-2601-18022: Tsao-Hsien Chen proves a duality result in the relative Langlands program. His 2026 preprint shows that the cotangent bundle of a quasi-split symmetric space matches a dual space. That dual is the variety of the loop symmetric space for the Langlands dual group. The result gives concrete cases of relative Langlands duality for non-split groups, a setting where such cases have been scarce.
arxiv-2601-18322:
A team of authors improves spatial audio capture for head-worn devices. Their 2026 preprint deals with neural Ambisonics encoders. Smart glasses and extended reality headsets need high-quality spatial sound from small microphone arrays worn on the head. Ambisonics is a device-agnostic format that maps array signals to spherical harmonic coefficients. In practice, accurate encoding from a compact array is hard. The authors use residual learning to help neural encoders do that mapping better.

Residual learning trains a network to fix the errors of a base estimate. Better encoding means more believable sound scenes for the wearer. Spatial audio sells immersion in calls, media, and assistive tech. The work targets a core step in that chain.
arxiv-2601-19122:
Weiran Guo and three co-authors hunt for weak spots in how models call outside tools. Function calling lets a language model use software tools and data feeds, a key skill for agents. Ways to train that skill rest on hand labeled or model made data, which may leave blind spots.

The team uses reinforcement learning to grow attack data that exposes those blind spots. Training against its own worst cases should harden the model where it truly fails. The loop mirrors how security teams probe a system: find the break, then teach against it.
arxiv-2601-19322:
Péter Salvi designs smooth surfaces that pass through every corner of a given mesh. A closed mesh of any topology sets the corners; the surface must interpolate them all. His method blends local patches, each a multi sided quadratic piece, into quadrilateral patches that join smoothly.

Faces with other than four sides need a special parameterization built from rational curves. Triangles among the subpatches get their own handling, with alternate forms discussed. Smooth through point surfaces serve design and animation, where a cage of points must become a skin that looks unbroken.
arxiv-2601-19422:
Moses Boudourides refines a classic network measure and ties it to how disease spreads. Newman's assortativity grades whether like nodes link to like. Boudourides splits that grade by a fixed partition of the nodes. Edges are classed by whether their ends sit inside a region or on its boundary.

The split yields interior boundary assortativity profiles, a finer structural fingerprint. He shows the profiles arise naturally from epidemic dynamics of the SIS kind on the network. A finer fingerprint could predict spread better, since where an edge sits, core or border, shapes how infection crosses between regions.
arxiv-2601-19522:
Jiadong Li, Hans-Walter Rix, and a large team of astronomers count the smallest stars in the oldest parts of our galaxy. Their target is the stellar mass function, which says how many stars are born at each mass. They focus on low-mass stars in regions poor in iron and other heavy elements. No one had measured this count for such metal-poor stars before.

Stars with few heavy elements formed early, when the galaxy was young. Their mass pattern is a fossil record of that era. The team reports the first determination of this function for such stars. The result tests ideas about how star formation changes with chemical makeup. It also sharpens the story of how the Milky Way built its oldest populations.
arxiv-2601-19622:
Thomas Bömer and four colleagues automate a craft inside search algorithms. A* search finds good paths by guessing, at each step, how much cost remains. That guess is the heuristic, and its quality decides how fast the search runs. Heuristics are usually handcrafted by experts, which takes time and skill.

The authors use large language models to design heuristics inside an evolutionary loop. Their twist is prompt augmentation: the prompts guiding the model are improved in a structured way. Better prompts should yield better candidate heuristics with less waste. The work tests how far this automated design can go. If it holds up, search tools could tune themselves for new problems.
arxiv-2601-19922:
Laya Iyer, Kriti Aggarwal, and colleagues build a benchmark for emotional support conversations. Supportive dialogue needs more than fluent language. A good supporter reads emotions, adjusts tone, and handles resistance, frustration, or distress. These skills decide whether a conversation actually helps.

Their benchmark, HEART, assesses humans and language models on the same footing. Putting both through identical tests exposes where models truly lag. It also shows where human supporters vary. Emotional support is a growing use of AI, in apps and helplines alike. A shared benchmark sets a bar for safety and quality. The work gives the field a common measure for a delicate task.
arxiv-2601-20322:
Martin Markl and Dominik Trnka prove a three-way equivalence in category theory, the abstract study of structures and maps. They show that a pointed category has kernels exactly when it is a lax algebra for the arrow 2-monad. They also show this holds exactly when the category is the décalage of a supercoherent structure.

The authors then read categories with kernels as the long-sought weak version of unary operadic categories. Equivalences like this let results move between fields: a fact proved in one language becomes usable in another. The paper ties homotopy-flavored algebra to concrete categorical structure.
arxiv-2601-20422:
Yumou Liu and five colleagues study paid promotion on content platforms and find a flaw in how it interacts with recommendation. Platforms offer promotion to cure cold start, giving new content exposure through auctions. The authors' empirical analysis shows promotion rescues low-to-medium quality content but can harm high-quality content.

Forced exposure to the wrong audiences pollutes the engagement signals that drive future recommendation, so good content gets downgraded. The authors build an information-aware auto-bidding method to guide the recommender instead. Their work shows promotion must be aimed, not just bought. Aimed well, the same spend can lift both reach and trust.
arxiv-2601-18522:
D. Alexander and four colleagues weigh how much the gas from farm stock warms the Earth. The gas, methane, leaks from the guts and dung of herd beasts. The team argue that its role in world heat is so small that it counts for next to nought. They back the claim with a thought test about the world's herd of cows.

In that test, to wipe out all cows on Earth at once would cut the gas by a share that moves world heat by a few hundredths of a degree. The team say such a small shift shows that herd gas is not a main driver of heat. The claim runs against the main view in climate work, and it is sure to draw sharp replies. Read it as one side of a live row, set out with its own sums.
arxiv-2601-18722:
Lintang Sutawika and three colleagues find a way to lift a model's thought in tongues it was barely trained on. When a hard ask comes in a rare tongue, scores drop far past the score for the same ask in English. That gap locks out much of the world from the best of these tools. The team use no fresh data in the rare tongue at all.

Their plan has the model play it-self in pairs. A judge twin, fed the English ask as a hid edge, grades pairs of tries in the rare tongue. The grades teach the model to pick its best line of thought, tongue by tongue. A lift with no new data is a prize for low-resource tongues. It could spread strong thought tools to lands they now skip.
arxiv-2601-21522:
Sagi Meir, Tommer D. Keidar, Noam Levi, Shlomi Reuveni, and Barak Hirshberg get more solved questions from a fixed budget of language model tries. The usual score counts a question as solved if any of many tries succeeds. With a fixed budget, a better score counts how many distinct questions get solved overall.

Their reset-and-discard method drops stalled attempts early and starts fresh ones. Wasted tries on one hopeless question can then fund progress on others. The metric they propose matches what users with real budgets care about. It rewards breadth of solved problems over deep grinding on a few.
arxiv-2601-21622:
Junhao He, Feiran You, and Hongyang Du scale speculative decoding across clusters of accelerators. The trick drafts tokens with a small fast model, then has the big model verify them. Most designs assume one machine, while modern serving spreads models over many nodes.

Their framework, StarSD, uses one draft model to serve many target models at once. The star layout links the single drafter to targets on distributed nodes. Sharing the drafter cuts wasted hardware across the cluster. Faster, cheaper generation matters as chat and coding tools serve millions of requests from shared data centers.
arxiv-2601-21722:
Neil Heinrich Braun, Keane Ong, Rui Mao, Erik Cambria, and Gianmarco Mengaldo harden language models for spotting greenwashing in company reports. Sustainability reports feed environmental and social scoring, yet vague claims often dress up thin action. Standard text models lean on surface patterns and fail on new wording.

The authors use an efficient framework that shapes the model's inner space with contrastive learning and an ordinal ranking goal. The ranking teaches graded steps between concrete action and empty talk. Sharper detection helps investors and regulators tell real progress from polished prose. It also pressures firms to report deeds, not adjectives.
arxiv-2601-22322:
Ayesh Abu Lehyeh, Anastassia Gharib, and Safwan Wshah aim to pin down where a device sits indoors, using Wi-Fi. Their 2026 preprint notes that GPS fails inside, yet apps for guidance, tracking, and safety need a firm fix. Graph models that link access points and devices give fine reads.

The gap they target is doubt: most tools give a point with no trust range. Their graph transformer adapts to each space and reports how sure it is. Honest doubt marks matter when a wrong fix has real costs. The method suits smart halls, stores, and clinics.
arxiv-2601-22122:
Omar Mohsen builds a new lens for equations that govern waves and heat on curved spaces. His 2026 preprint starts from a set of vector fields that meet a classic reach rule, named for Hörmander. He defines a calculus with two grades, built to fit both the plain case and a bent, sub-Riemannian one.

The build rests on geometry, with a blow-up trick to untangle stuck points, plus tools from operator algebras. The goal is the strongest smooth-out claim the setup allows. Such claims tell us when rough inputs still yield smooth outputs. The work is part one of a planned series.
arxiv-2601-22422:
Jie Mei and four co-authors work out how pion particles behave inside a strong magnetic field. Pions are light particles made of quarks, key to the strong force. Their 2026 preprint uses a standard quark model, the NJL model, with a method built for charged particles in fields.

They treat both neutral and charged pions, and weigh heat and symmetry effects too. Such extreme settings echo the early cosmos and dense stars. Knowing pion traits there helps decode signals from both. The work is theory, done with care. It maps a small but telling corner of the strong force.
arxiv-2601-22522:
Zhou Tang and a large team test whether 3D point clouds can grade a dairy cow's body condition on their own. Body condition scores track a cow's fat and health, and guide feeding. Their 2026 preprint asks if depth-based shape data beat flat images for auto scoring.

Point clouds hold the true curve of the back and hips, where fat shows. A sound auto score saves labor and catches health slips early. The team weigh the added worth of the depth data. The work fits precision farming, where each cow's state counts. It is a clear, practical test.
arxiv-2601-22622:
Andrés Solís-Cuevas and Pablo Vázquez-Montejo work out how a round fluid vesicle dents when a stiff ring grips its equator. A vesicle is a tiny bubble of fluid film, like a simple cell wall. Their 2026 preprint stays in the linear regime, where the dent is small.

They solve the governing equation in closed form, holding area and volume fixed, with the ring as a local rule. The solution shows how the bubble trades shape for the grip. Such models aid lab work on cells and capsules. They also give a clean check for simulations. The work is exact and spare.
arxiv-2601-22022:
J. Baños-Gutiérrez and co-authors study groups where light and matter merge into one. Each group joins a tiny silver particle with dye molecules called TDBC. The particle traps light in a very small space. The dye gives off light at a set color. When the two sit close, they link so strongly that the light and the dye act as one thing.

The team looks at three things: how the dye is built, how it sticks to the silver, and how messy the groups are. Real groups are never neat, and mess changes how they act. This work helps those who build new sensors and new light sources. It shows what these mixed groups need to work well in real life, not just in clean lab tests.
arxiv-2601-20722:
Milan van Zanten writes about portals in virtual reality in this 2026 paper. A portal is a window or door that links one space to another. In computer graphics, portals have long had many uses. They can show which parts of a 3D scene are visible. They can split a scene into separate areas. They can also act as mirrors.

Van Zanten focuses on the kind of portal a user can see and step through. In VR, such a portal must be drawn so the view stays smooth and true. The paper explains how these views are rendered. It covers the graphics ideas that make a doorway into another world look right. For VR builders, it is a clear guide to a classic trick of the trade.
arxiv-2601-20822:
Mohammadali Mohammadi and four co-authors study a wireless network boosted by simple relay boxes. Their 2026 paper concerns repeater-assisted massive MIMO with full-duplex links. Massive MIMO uses a base station with very many antennas. Repeaters amplify what they hear and re-send it at once. Full-duplex means sending and receiving share the same frequency band at the same time.

In their setup, each repeater has a single antenna. The base station serves many users at once, some sending up and some receiving down. All of this happens over one band, which is hard to keep clean. The paper analyzes how such a network performs. Repeaters are cheap and simple, so the design could raise capacity without new towers. The work speaks to the design of dense future wireless networks.
arxiv-2601-20922:
Luis Sánchez-Soto, Andrei Klimov, Aaron Goldberg, and Gerd Leuchs present a sky-like way to picture quantum spin states. Their 2026 paper concerns Majorana stars. A spin state can be drawn as a set of points, its stars, on a sphere. For a spin-S state, the stars number twice S. Some stars are defined as the coherent states orthogonal to the given state. The picture turns algebra into geometry.

The authors call this map the quantum sky of Majorana stars. The representation offers insight into structure, symmetries, and entanglement. It bridges abstract formulas with intuitive pictures. A reader can see symmetry as a pattern of points. Entanglement shows up in how the stars arrange themselves. The paper serves physicists who teach or reason about spin. It refreshes a classic visualization with a modern treatment.
arxiv-2601-21122:
Jeremy Tanlimco and six co-authors build a cavity for matter waves driven to an extreme. Their 2026 paper studies a matter-wave Fabry-Pérot cavity in the ultrastrong driving regime. When an optical cavity's length is modulated, theory predicts a striking effect. Energy concentrates exponentially around particular space-time trajectories. Viewed stroboscopically, photons inside propagate as if in curved spacetime. Black hole and white hole horizons appear as fixed points of the motion.

The authors realize the same drama with atoms instead of light. Matter waves replace photons in the driven cavity. Ultrastrong driving pushes the system far beyond gentle shaking. Stable and unstable fixed points mimic horizons. Such analog systems let labs probe curved-spacetime physics on a bench. The paper extends a rich analogy between optics, atoms, and gravity.
arxiv-2512-01422:
Yongkun Du and co-authors bring mask diffusion models to scene text reading. Reading text in wild photos is hard. Letters bend, blur, and mix with busy scenes. Most top readers build text one letter at a time, in order.

Mask diffusion works in a distinct way. It starts with masked text and fills it in steps. That gives a good mix of speed and care. The team is the first to use it for scene text. Their model, MDiff4STR, aims for sharp reads on signs, labels, and plates in real photos.
arxiv-2512-01722:
Borsoni introduces folded optimal transport for costs defined on extreme points. Optimal transport moves mass at least cost. Costs are often known only on the boundary extremes of a convex set. The whole set still needs a cost for real tasks.

Folding extends that boundary cost to the full set by a convex route. Standard transport returns as the case where the set is a simplex. The build also serves separable quantum transport tasks. A broader frame unifies tasks in economics, imaging, and quantum information. Separable quantum costs fit the fold cleanly, which links the new build to entanglement measures that transport theory already serves.
arxiv-2512-00722:
Jiaming Xu and six coauthors address a cost problem in large language models in their 2025 paper, SpeContext. Reasoning models now write long step-by-step answers, which improves their work. The catch is memory: long outputs build a large key-value cache that stores past context for the model.

That cache becomes a bottleneck when such models run in real products, such as software agents. SpeContext uses speculative context sparsity, keeping only the parts of context that matter most. Guessing well about what can be thinned out could cut memory sharply. If quality holds, long reasoning becomes cheaper to serve at scale.
arxiv-2512-01022:
Yi-Lin Wei and six coauthors open a new task in robot manipulation in a 2025 paper. Many daily jobs are cyclic: shaking a bottle, knocking a nail, or stirring in rounds. The robot must repeat an action and stop at an expected terminal time, which adds a timing demand most manipulation work ignores.

Their system, CycleManip, enables cyclic task manipulation. It leans on effective historical perception and understanding, meaning the robot tracks what it has already done in the cycle. Counting repetitions from vision is easy for people and hard for machines. A robot that tracks cycles could handle chores and assembly steps more reliably.
arxiv-2512-01222:
Ching Fang and Samuel Marks probe hidden reasoning in language models in a 2025 paper. As models grow more capable, there is concern they may develop reasoning that is encoded or hidden from human oversight. Checking whether interpretability tools can penetrate such reasoning is an open safety question.

The authors build a controlled testbed for the problem. They fine-tune a reasoning model to do its chain-of-thought in ROT-13, a simple letter-shifting cipher, while keeping its final outputs in plain English. They then test unsupervised decoding methods from interpretability research. The setup shows whether today's tools can recover reasoning that a model has disguised.
arxiv-2601-22922:
Sachin Chauhan, Tobias Ekholm, and Pietro Longhi connect knot theory with the counting of holomorphic curves. They study open strings on the complement of a fibered knot, the space left when a knot is removed. Their counting uses skein-valued methods, which keep track of richer algebraic data than plain numbers.

The result is a flow loop formula for the skein-valued partition function in two settings. One is the cotangent bundle of the three-sphere, and the other is the resolved conifold. Such formulas tie knot invariants to string theory in a precise way.
arxiv-2601-23022:
Lung-Hao Lee and a large team build datasets for finer-grained sentiment analysis. Aspect-based sentiment analysis rates feelings toward specific aspects of a product or service. Older datasets use coarse labels like positive or negative, which miss the strength and shade of a feeling.

Their DimABSA datasets rate sentiment along dimensions instead, across many languages and domains. Dimensional labels capture mixed, graded opinions far better than three boxes. Richer benchmarks should push review analysis closer to how people really express views. Dimensional labels replace the old positive-or-negative boxes, recording sentiment strength along continuous scales for each aspect.
arxiv-2601-23222:
Hamza Kalisch and four co-authors train medical image segmentation without costly pixel-level labels. Dense annotations are the gold standard, but they are expensive and limit scale. Deployed systems already emit cheap quality signals, like model agreement and uncertainty scores.

Their region-normalized preference method learns from those noisy judges instead of ground truth. Normalizing by region keeps large and small structures treated fairly. Training from existing quality signals could scale segmentation to hospitals without annotation teams. Model agreement, uncertainty measures, and learned mask-quality scores are the inexpensive signals the method learns from instead of annotations.
arxiv-2512-00122:
National pension plans pool everyone together, which can be unfair to groups with shorter life expectancies. Moshe Milevsky, Thomas Salisbury, and Robyn Allen examine that tension in a 2025 study. They ask whether high-mortality groups might prefer pension pools aligned with their own demographics.

The authors call such arrangements equitable longevity risk sharing pools, using a First Nations pension plan as the motivating case. Joining a separate pool means giving up some guarantees and accepting more individual risk. The study weighs that trade-off, offering actuaries and policymakers a framework for fairer retirement design. Pension design rarely faces this trade-off so directly, which gives the study its force.
arxiv-2512-00422:
Generative models can design three-dimensional shapes that look plausible yet fail as real products. Yingxuan You and co-authors present PhysGen in 2025, a framework for physically grounded shape generation aimed at industrial design. For engineered shapes, realism is tied to physical properties like aerodynamic efficiency.

A car body that ignores airflow may render beautifully and still be a bad design. PhysGen couples shape generation to the underlying physics so outputs respect engineering constraints. Designers could explore more concepts automatically while keeping each candidate grounded in how the object must actually perform. Industrial design is the test case, where a pretty shape that fails physics is worthless. Automobiles are the running example, since drag decides their efficiency.
arxiv-2512-00622:
Force feedback gloves let virtual reality users feel resistance, but most designs fit one hand size and one task. Pablo Alvarez Romeo and Mehmet Ercan Altinsoy present KinesCeTI in 2025, a modular force feedback glove with interchangeable actuation for the index finger and thumb. Adaptability is the design's central claim.

Limited adaptability, simplified feedback, and fixed architectures have constrained earlier gloves. A size-adaptable exoskeleton with swappable actuators serves more users and more applications, from rehabilitation to remote operation. Better haptics close the loop between seeing a virtual object and truly handling it. Interchangeable actuation lets one glove serve gripping, therapy, and training tasks. The index and thumb do most precision work, so they are the natural focus.
arxiv-2512-03122:
Fitting math models of living systems to data is a hard task. Piotr Gwiazda, Alexey Kazarnikov, Anna Marciniak-Czochra, and Zuzanna Szymańska survey ways to do it in this 2025 work. Good fits are key for sound forecasts and for insight into how life works.

Data are often scarce and noisy, and living systems vary a lot. The models, based on partial differential equations, are also costly to run. The authors go beyond standard Bayesian methods and test a new likelihood framework with gradient flow tools. Their guide helps modelers pick methods for real biological problems. Their framework serves PDE models in biology, where data limits rule out many classic methods.
arxiv-2512-03322:
Learning from partly labeled data is common in real studies. Geoffrey McLachlan and Jinran Wu present an R package for that task in this 2025 work. Labels often need expert judgment or costly hand work, so most data stay unlabeled.

Their package, SSLfmm, works with finite mixture models, which view data as blends of groups. It also handles data missing in mixed ways. Semi-supervised methods that use unlabeled cases can sharpen classifiers a lot. A ready R package puts those methods in reach of working statisticians. Mixture models suit partly labeled data, since groups can absorb unlabeled cases naturally.
arxiv-2512-02622:
Xuming He and nine co-authors test whether video generators follow rules, not just look pretty. New video models hold together over time and look impressive, a step toward vision foundation models. Most benchmarks grade beauty, instruction following, and smoothness, which leaves rule based reasoning unchecked.

RULER-Bench probes whether generated videos obey stated physical and logical rules. A model can look right frame by frame while breaking the rule that binds the scene. Testing rules directly helps builders find where video models merely imitate, and where they truly grasp how a scene should unfold. Rules are a stern test: a clip can look smooth and still break the one rule that counts most.
arxiv-2512-02722:
Matteo Tolloso and Davide Bacciu give graph neural networks a new way to express doubt. Such networks learn from linked data, and honest uncertainty is essential before trusting them in practice. Most current tools rely on Bayesian inference or on ensembles of models.

Their credal graph neural networks output sets of plausible predictions instead of one fixed answer. A credal set shows the range the model still finds credible. Set valued answers can warn users when a graph based system, used in science or medicine, is guessing beyond its evidence. A set of live picks is a more honest brief than one pick dressed up as sure fact for a board.
arxiv-2512-03022:
Ranadeep Roy and Wei Chen compute a topological marker in three dimensions without the usual crushing cost. A universal topological marker measures how disorder affects topological order at the atomic scale. In higher dimensions, direct calculation of the marker becomes numerically very costly.

Their method applies the kernel polynomial method, which expands the needed quantities in fast polynomial series. They argue it works efficiently for any symmetry class in higher dimensions. Cheap markers let researchers screen disordered topological materials on a computer before growing crystals in a lab. Cheap marks let teams scan whole fields of stuff for the rare good one. Hand work can not do that at the scale new finds now demand of them in the lab.
plos-pone-0010022:
Fotios Drenos and Thomas Kirkwood took on a common claim about aging genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The claim says genes that harm health late in life escape natural selection, because their effects come after breeding age. Apolipoprotein E is a prime case, since its variants affect heart disease and Alzheimer's disease risk.

Using a simulation built on known genetic and lifestyle risk factors, the authors tested that claim directly. Factors in the model included sex, diet, smoking, and alcohol use. Their work shows late-life effects may not sit safely beyond selection after all, which changes how aging genetics can be read.
plos-pone-0010222:
The authors were Jeremy Driskell, Yu Zhu, Carl Kirkwood, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a fast test for rotavirus, a common gut virus. Gut viruses range from mild stomach illness to life-threatening disease. Rotavirus kills many children in developing countries, so quick, sensitive detection matters where lab resources are thin and illness spreads fast.

Their method uses surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy, a light-based fingerprint technique. It reads molecular signatures of the virus rapidly and with high sensitivity. A field-ready version could speed diagnosis during outbreaks and guide care for sick children.
plos-pone-0010322:
Paul Cross, Dennis Heisey, Brandon Scurlock and others tackled brucellosis in elk for PLOS ONE in 2010. Brucellosis is a bacterial disease that can pass from wild animals to livestock. Managers often assume that more host animals means faster spread. Yet hard numbers for that link in big wild mammals were scarce. The authors set out to estimate it from field data.

They used layered Bayesian models, a method that blends past knowledge with new counts. The models mapped where the disease was rising against how dense elk herds were. That kind of map helps officials choose where to focus control work. It also tests a core idea behind many wildlife disease plans. Crowding, in short, is treated here as a measurable risk, not a guess.
plos-pone-0009822:
Growing nerves must cross the midline of the nervous system in the right pattern. Joy Dorsten and colleagues studied what goes wrong when a guidance gene is missing in embryos. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The missing gene is frazzled, which normally helps axons decide where to grow. Without it, extra Abelson tyrosine kinase disrupted commissure formation, the bridges axons build across the midline. Some axons even left the embryonic central nervous system entirely. The result shows how two signals balance each other during wiring. Embryos build the nervous system step by step.
plos-pone-0009922:
Leaf-cutter ants farm fungus for food, and their gardens host whole microbial worlds. Jarrod Scott and colleagues mapped the microbial community in those gardens and in the ants' refuse dumps. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Microbial community structure means which microbes live there and in what shares. The fungus gardens are tended chambers where ants grow their crop. Refuse dumps hold the spent material the ants throw out. Comparing the two shows how ants manage microbes, friend and foe alike. The ants cut leaves not to eat, but to feed their fungus.
